#5077. Walking This Many Steps a Day Could Help Lower Your Risk of Alzheimers—It’s Less Than You Think

You've probably heard by now that exercising regularly is good for your brain and may even help lower your risk of Alzheimer's disease. But new research suggests that you don't have to kill yourself at the gym to harness these perks.

The study, which was published in Nature Medicine last year but is making the rounds now, found that taking just 3,000 steps a day is linked to significantly lower rates of cognitive decline, along with fewer markers of Alzheimer's disease.

It's worth pointing out that 3,000 steps isn't a ton (we're talking about walking about 1.5 miles in a day). That makes this a very doable goal to aim for. But how accurate is this, and what does it suggest about the 10,000-step goal everyone throws around? Doctors weigh in.

Meet the experts: Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center; Nikhil Satchidanand, PhD, a research assistant professor of medicine in the Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences at the University at Buffalo; Liron Sinvani, MD, director of research and innovation for the Institute for Healthy Aging at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research; Anna Hohler, MD, regional director of Neurology for Westchester, Northwell Health, and chair of Neurology for Northern Westchester and Phelps hospitals; and Shannel Elhelou, PsyD, a neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, California.

For the observational study, researchers analyzed data from 296 people between the ages of 50 and 90 who participated in the Harvard Aging Brain Study, a long-running study that tracks brain changes in older adults. None of the participants had dementia or signs of cognitive decline at the start of the study.

Participants wore waistband pedometers to track their physical activity and underwent PET brain scans to measure the amount of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles (both are hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease). Participants also underwent cognitive assessment about 9.3 years later.

The researchers found that people who had higher step counts also had lower rates of cognitive decline. Higher step counts were also linked with a slower buildup of tau. Not only that, but walking 3,000 to 5,000 steps daily seemed to slow progression of Alzheimer's disease in people who were at a higher risk of developing it.

Specifically, those considered high risk for Alzheimer's disease who walked 3,000 to 5,000 steps a day had a three-year delay in developing cognitive decline. People who walked 5,000 to 7,500 steps daily saw a seven-year delay in their cognitive decline.

Those who were more sedentary saw a buildup of tau proteins in the brain, along with faster rates of decline in their cognition and daily functioning.

There are probably a few things behind this, according to neurologists. A big one is that physical activity is simply good for the brain. "It improves blood flow, supports cardiovascular and metabolic health, reduces systemic inflammation, and may help protect brain cells from aging-related damage," says Nikhil Satchidanand, PhD, research assistant professor of medicine in the Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences at the University at Buffalo.

Working out also helps stimulate the release of protective molecules like irisin and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which support the health and connectivity of brain cells, says Liron Sinvani, MD, director of research and innovation for the Institute for Healthy Aging at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research. "Exercise also improves cardiovascular fitness, and what is good for the heart is good for the brain," she adds. Daily walks can support your cardiovascular system and may lower the risk of vascular or multi-infarct dementia, according to Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center.

Neurologists applaud how approachable the findings are. "Importantly, 3,000 steps is an achievable goal for many people, making regular physical activity more sustainable over time," says Anna Hohler, MD, regional director of Neurology for Westchester, Northwell Health, and chair of Neurology for Northern Westchester and Phelps hospitals. "Consistent movement, even at lower levels, appears to contribute to better cognitive resilience and may help reduce the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease."

But Dr. Satchidanand says that "there's nothing magical" about 3,000 steps. "The brain doesn't suddenly start benefiting from physical activity when someone reaches a particular number of daily steps," he says. "The relationship between physical activity and health exists along a continuum."

Step count also only reveals one dimension of a person's physical activity, Dr. Satchidanand says. "They don't tell us much about walking intensity, cardiovascular fitness, strength training, or other forms of movement that may also influence brain health," he says.

Dr. Satchidanand says it's also important to consider that people who develop Alzheimer's disease may move less, which could also influence findings. "Early Alzheimer's-related changes in the brain could themselves lead people to become less physically active, even before noticeable cognitive symptoms develop," he points out.

The idea that you only need to log 3,000 steps a day to slow down cognitive decline is definitely appealing—and far less than the 10,000-step milestone that gets thrown around a lot. So where does that magical 10,000 standard come from?

Turns out, it’s actually an arbitrary number from a marketing campaign for a Japanese step counter. Since then, research has actually suggested that 10,000 steps is more than most people need to be healthy. So, if you want to walk that many steps a day, more power to you—but just know you don’t actually need to walk that far to reap health benefits.

Movement in general benefits the brain, so it’s hard to go wrong if you find something you love.

"My advice is to find activities you enjoy and can realistically sustain," says Shannel Elhelou, PsyD, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, California. "Consistency matters, and an achievable routine can grow over time."

This can include brisk walking, swimming, dancing, or cycling, depending on your abilities and preferences, Elhelou says. "I also encourage people to consider what makes movement meaningful to them," she continues.

Dr. Satchidanand also notes that people shouldn't feel boxed in by a specific step count. "Moving more, particularly among people who are currently inactive, is beneficial for overall health and may help support healthier brain aging," he says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

Block raised its full-year gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, which would represent a 22% year-on-year growth.

Jack Dorsey-led fintech firm Block Inc. Block, Inc. (XYZ) saw its shares jump 6.2% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after reporting stronger third-quarter earnings and raising its full-year profit outlook.

Block posted a net income of $566 million in the third quarter of this year, up from $462 million a year earlier, according to its latest quarterly report released Tuesday. It generated $6.72 billion in total revenue, up from $6.12 billion in the same quarter last year.

The company's gross profit rose 22% year-on-year to $3.24 billion, while its Cash App booked $2.07 billion in gross profit, up 27% year-on-year.

On the back of the results, Block raised its full-year gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, representing a 22% year-on-year growth.

"We are raising our full-year guidance to reflect the momentum we are seeing across Block," the company said. Block said it expects gross profit to grow at least 15% in 2027, as it continues to "expand margins while still investing meaningfully to sustain long-term growth."

Block shares closed down 1.4% at $76 on Tuesday but jumped 6.2% in after-hours trading following the earnings release.

Meanwhile, the firm's bitcoin ecosystem gross profit fell 50% year-over-year to $52 million in the third quarter, according to the report.

It attributed the decline to its "strategic decision to reduce the fee" charged on certain bitcoin transactions on Cash App. Block's bitcoin ecosystem primarily consists of customer purchases of bitcoin within Cash App, Proto, as well as bitcoin withdrawal fees, per the report.

#5075. Democrats claim control of the US Senate

The shift in Senate control could change the path for the CLARITY Act, reshape committee leadership and bring closer scrutiny of Trump’s crypto businesses.

Democrats have won control of the US Senate after flipping Republican-held seats in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa, according to the Associated Press.

The majority was secured after Democrat Senator Josh Turek won the Senate race for Iowa, bringing Democrats and independents who caucus with them to 51 seats.

The result reshapes the outlook for the stalled CLARITY Act and determines which lawmakers lead committees overseeing the industry.

Democratic control could also bring more congressional scrutiny of Trump-linked crypto businesses and regulators’ decisions. Control of the Senate could also affect confirmation of future presidential nominees to regulatory posts.

“It’s too early to say exactly what this means for crypto, but one thing is clear: nothing will pass without cross-partisan support,” Jerome de Tychey, president of Ethereum France and co-founder of EthCC, told Cointelegraph.

“The CLARITY Act failed its Senate procedural vote 49 to 50 in September, and if it isn’t passed by January, the next Congress starts again from scratch. So the industry will have to go back to the table and make the case for blockchain again, on substance.”

De Tychey said some Democratic demands could help strengthen the industry’s regulatory framework.

“Conflict-of-interest rules and customer protection obligations are things a mature industry should welcome. In Europe, we already live with them under MiCA,” he said, referring to the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation.

However, he warned against allowing crypto policy to become entrenched along party lines.

“The biggest risk for crypto in America is for it to become entrenched as a partisan issue; that could set the US back several years.”

Fred Hsu, co-founder and CEO of D3, a core contributor to Doma Protocol, similarly said durable regulation would require support from both parties.

“The midterms are a good reminder that the industry can’t rely on one party to deliver them, and should be making its case to lawmakers on both sides now,” Hsu said in comments provided ahead of the election.

#5074. The 8 Best Slip-On Walking Shoes, According to Our Editors

Looking to get out the door quicker? Don’t let laces slip you up.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

SLIDING INTO A pair of slip-on walking shoes might be the easiest thing you’ll do all day. This footwear was built for speed and convenience, making it an accessory that deserves valuable real estate by your door.

Slip-on walking shoes have a rocky history—older versions had a looser fit, raising the risk of instability and friction, especially with higher mileage. But newer designs use no-tie laces, sock liners, pull tabs, and collapsible heels to create a custom fit that rivals what you’ll get with traditional laces.

These shoes are an obvious choice if you have dexterity issues, but they're also just convenient for everyone looking for an easy pair of walking shoes. Slip-on walking shoes also offer more structure than other laceless shoe designs, which has earned them a fanbase with podiatrists. “They are typically a much better option than flip-flops or slides because they provide more stability and keep the foot properly secured,” says Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois.

Nicole Graf, DPM, founder of Lexington Podiatry and associate professor at the University of Kentucky, also calls slip-on walking shoes a “huge step up” from flip-flops and slides.

Slip-on walking shoes aren’t for everyone. The fit can still throw some people off, and some simply prefer the tighter feel that laces deliver. But if you want travel-friendly shoes you can toss on in a second, these are a solid choice. As people who value quality, supportive footwear, Men’s Health editors have put in plenty of miles in slip-on walking shoes. The below check all the boxes.

The On Cloud 6 is an excellent example of how good a slip-on shoe can be. You can get in and out of this sneaker with no issue thanks to its wide opening, but the shoe’s elastic “speed” laces and sockliner create a snug fit once you’re in. (Those elastic laces can be adjusted to find your perfect fit.)

The sneaker uses Zero-Gravity CloudTec, which is On’s signature lightweight foam with hollow pods below for a cushioned, yet stable, feel underfoot. (Just be aware that those pods are prone to trapping small pebbles and debris.) A built-in flexible plate, called a Speedboard, helps push you forward with each step. This shoe also comes in a waterproof option, if you’re into rainy strolls. With a wide range of color options and an unobnoxious design, you can pair these with just about anything.

It’s tough to find a quality shoe under $100 right now, let alone one from a big brand. But the Adidas Cloudfoam Cuxxion Sock Shoes have some colorways under $50, making them an ideal choice for budget shoppers who don’t want to mess with laces.

This shoe uses Adidas’ signature Cloudfoam technology at the midsole for a plush, cushioned feel. Its Adiwear outsole is durable and grippy enough for most needs, too. But the real standout in this shoe is its elastic sock upper. It molds to your foot to create a surprisingly snug feel, even for narrow feet. The elastic sock collar supports that secure feel, although it may be too tight for people with wider ankles. The engineered knit upper is highly breathable, lowering the odds you’ll end your walk with sweaty feet. We appreciate the oversized pull tabs in front and back, making the process of getting these on and off seamless.

Feet come in all sizes, making it tough to find a slip-on shoe that works for everyone—and putting adjustable features at a premium. The Nike Pegasus 42 EasyOn has a specialized EasyOn lacing and bungee system up top to help you get the level of tightness you want, before locking it into place. (The lock and bungee combination takes some practice to get right at first.)

The shoe has a collapsible heel that springs back into place once you’re in, making the process of getting these on seamless. It’s also crafted with the same ReactX foam and Air Zoom unit as the standard—and popular—Nike Pegasus 42 running shoe, delivering an energetic feel under your feet. Convenient pull tabs at the heel sit flush against the shoe when they’re not in use, adding to the shoe’s overall sleekness.

Read More: Best Walking Shoes for Men Over 50

Stability shoes are designed to guide your foot with each step and prevent too much inward rolling as you go. But choosing a stability shoe usually means sacrificing a high level of cushioning, since a shoe that feels too plush may not be overly supportive. Hoka’s Skyward Laceless manages to create a stable, locked-in feel while still delivering plenty of the brand’s signature cushioning underfoot.

The Skyward Laceless has a stretchy upper that gently hugs your foot, creating a sock-like feel. The ankle and instep are equally snug, which can be a good or bad thing, depending on your foot size and width. This shoe has plenty of foam below for a slightly bouncy feel, but it still corrects your stride as you go. The integrated tongue pull tab is a nice touch, making for easier entry.

The Under Armour SlipSpeed Mega is packed with features you won’t find in most slip-on walking shoes, creating a versatile, unique sneaker. For starters, this shoe converts from a sneaker design to a recovery slipper with the help of a collapsible heel. (Under Armour refers to this as going from “speed mode” to “slip mode.”)

The shoe skips elastic laces or a sockliner upper in favor of Under Armour’s specialized BOA fit system, a 12-point dial that you can turn to adjust the width across the midfoot. The wide base creates a stable feel, while lots of foam cushioning underfoot delivers a plushness you’ll appreciate. A heads-up: This shoe is slightly heavier than others at 11.7 ounces. That’s a difference you may start to feel on long walks.

After a grueling workout, it feels borderline pampering to slide into the right recovery shoe. The Kane Footwear Active Recovery Shoe is armed with features that should make it a fixture in your gym bag.

This slip-on has strong arch support and a slight rocker shape to help ease pressure on the bottom of your feet as you walk. Internal nodes in the footbed help to promote blood flow and circulation down below, while the shoe’s surprisingly secure design helps prevent slipping. The Active Recovery Shoe is water-resistant with an airy design that allows you to take this in and out of the gym shower without ending up with sopping feet. Heel tabs in back make it simple to get in and out.

Merrell is known for its rugged, outdoor footwear and hiking shoes. While the Merrell Jungle Moc isn’t exactly a hiking shoe, it’s a solid option when you want good traction, whether you’re navigating rocky ground or a slippery surface. The Jungle Moc has been a bestseller for years, with its simple slip-on design and high level of cushioning.

Dual side stretch panels and an exaggerated heel tab make it simple to get in and out of these shoes. The suede upper is breathable, but water-resistant to keep you dry in nearly all conditions. The Jungle Moc has a cushioned EVA midsole for stability and comfort, too. While these shoes are easy to get on, the curved heel makes it harder to slide out—just something to be aware of.

Clogs admittedly aren’t the right style for everyone—some offer less support than sneakers and may slip around more than a standard shoe. But the sleek Crocs Dylan Clog is a solid option for people who want a clog style without some of the common issues that come with it.

The Dylan Clog has a deep heel cup to help lock your foot in, lowering the risk it’ll move around as you step. It’s also made from one piece of Croslite (Crocs’ signature material) to prevent wear and tear over time. This shoe looks like leather thanks to its subtle pebbled texture, but it’s water-resistant and dries quickly when wet. The only major downside is that it’s not very breathable in front. If you’re prone to sweaty toes, this may not be the shoe for you.

Not all shoes are created equal, but the best slip-on walking shoes have all of the supportive features you’ll find in standard lace-up walking shoes. “You mostly get what you pay for in these,” says Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California. He suggests taking a pass at dirt-cheap slip-on walking shoes. “The cheaper ones are not going to provide enough support in the long run, even if they might feel good at first,” Graves says. “There should be enough structure to support your arch and the midsole should be firm and not too flimsy.”

Many high-quality slip-on walking shoes provide similar comfort to regular sneakers. Look for elements like a breathable upper, pull tabs to make them easy to get on and off, and a roomy toe box. Structured heel panels and extra padding in this area help to keep your foot secure, even without standard laces.

Traction for slip-on walking shoes will vary depending on the type of shoe you choose. Most will offer decent traction—meaning, enough so you don’t feel like you’re slipping on wet or damp pavement. But a more rugged shoe like the Merrell Jungle Moc has a grippier sole to help provide extra traction over rockier ground.

Yes, slip-on walking shoes can provide arch support. If this is an important quality for you, look for features like contoured footbeds and a stable midsole. You’ll also want a shoe that fits well and stays put once it’s on to ensure your arch support is consistent. “Make sure that you're not getting them too loose just to make it easier to slide on and off—then you'll be sacrificing support,” Graves says.

To find the best men’s slip-on walking shoes, MH editors tested the most recent and popular pairs on the market, evaluating each for support, comfort, and traction. Because these shoes are designed for walking, not just comfort, durability was also a key factor. #5073. Why Am I Always So Tired? 15 Reasons You May Have Fatigue

Allergies, stress, and sugar could all play a part in your energy levels.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The most relatable statement of all time: “I’m exhausted.” Life is stressful, busy, and often feels like an impossible balancing act. Beyond the demands of endless work tasks and social obligations, legit health reasons could explain lingering fatigue. If you’re chugging coffee on the regular and still wondering, Why am I so tired? it's worth considering whether something in your body is causing your low energy.

Obviously, if you stay up binging a new series or push yourself harder than usual while training for an upcoming race, you’re gonna feel sluggish the next day. But there’s a difference between feeling tapped out sometimes and long bouts of fatigue that won’t go away.

Meet the experts: Antoinette LaDawn Price, MD, MPH, is a family medicine doctor at Emory Physician Group Practice; Purvi Parikh, MD, is an allergist and immunologist with Allergy & Asthma Network; Sobia Khan, MD, is the director of Women's Center for Comprehensive Care at Baylor College of Medicine; Jessica Cording, RD, is the author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; Monifa Seawell, MD, is a board-certified psychiatrist in Atlanta, Georgia

“Fatigue is chronic extreme tiredness,” says Antoinette LaDawn Price, MD, MPH, at Emory Physician Group Practice. Fatigue can show up as headaches, dizziness, and achy and sore muscles, irritability, brain fog, and moodiness; it manifests differently in each person.

If you always feel drained, it may be time for you to consult your doctor about your symptoms. If you feel like something is off, don’t ignore it—there are many health issues, both mental and physical, that can make it difficult for you to last through the entire day without wanting to collapse in bed. Here are possible causes of fatigue, according to doctors.

Classic symptoms of seasonal allergies include sneezing and having watery eyes. Less common symptoms include low energy and fatigue. “If left untreated, seasonal allergies can cause fatigue,” says Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with Allergy & Asthma Network. Why? Your body works hard to fend off the allergen, and that takes extra energy. That’s true whether you're allergic to outdoor triggers like ragweed or pollen, or to indoor allergens like dust mites, Dr. Parikh says.

Allergens aren’t the only things that can trigger fatigue—allergy medications can, too. “Some of the over-the-counter allergy pills like antihistamines unfortunately cause fatigue as well,” says Dr. Parikh.

How to fix it: If allergies leave you feeling completely spent, your current treatment plan may not be working. So, check in with your doctor about your options. They’ll likely recommend medication (or a different one) to help get things under control. Running a HEPA air purifier at home can also help clear the air, notes Dr. Parikh.

While going hard during your at-home workouts can wear you out, the opposite can do the same. “The human body gets more tired with progressive sedentary habits due to generalized reconditioning of the body and, ultimately, muscle loss,” explains Sobia Khan, MD, an assistant professor of general internal medicine and the director of Women's Center for Comprehensive Care at Baylor College of Medicine.

Basically, your body takes a “use it or lose it” approach to fitness. If you don’t exercise regularly, you’ll feel more tired when you start moving and even when you’re at rest.

How to fix it: This solution is pretty simple—get moving more. Just a reminder, the general physical activity recommendation is 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise each week, plus muscle-strengthening activity at least two days a week. Once you start moving again, it’ll be easier to get through your day-to-day stuff without being a zombie.

When you eat sugary foods or foods high in refined carbs (think: white bread, pasta, pastries), your blood sugar spikes, according to Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. In the moment, that can make you feel kinda hyper. But unfortunately, you're also in for an inevitable crash, which can leave you feeling totally wiped.

If you keep overloading on sugar and refined carbs, you may also develop insulin resistance, Dr. Khan adds. That is when your body can’t use glucose (a.k.a. sugar) as well as it should for energy.

How to fix it: Cording says to cut back on sugar and refined carbs regularly. FWIW, the CDC recommends limiting added sugar to less than 10 percent of your total daily calories. (So, if you eat a 2,000-calorie diet, no more than 200 of those calories should come from added sugars.)

When you’re having sugary or carb-heavy foods, balance the meal with protein and fat, like adding nut butter to your crackers. This can help lower the odds that you’ll crash afterward, Cording says.

Stress isn’t just mental—it can affect you physically, too. “Your mind and body are closely linked and are in constant communication with one another,” says Monifa Seawell, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist in Atlanta, Georgia. “When there is a shift in your emotional state, be it positive or negative, it is not at all uncommon for that change to also show up in some physical way in your body.”

You can start getting headaches, an upset stomach, and, yep, fatigue, Dr. Seawell says.

How to fix it: The best approach is to address the root of your stress. While some stressors are unavoidable, doing your utmost to limit the ones you can address can be helpful.

Dr. Seawell also recommends scheduling 20 to 30 minutes of exercise each day. She says this can often boost your energy levels when you can’t completely eliminate your stress. If you’re still struggling, try talking to a licensed mental health professional. They “can help you process your emotions and learn healthy coping skills,” Dr. Seawell says.

Adults should be getting seven hours or more a night, according to the CDC. Definitely getting less? Enter: Fatigue.

“Minimum seven hours of sleep is required for effective rejuvenation of the body and restfulness of the brain,” says Dr. Khan. Here’s the thing: Even one night of bad sleep can mess with your circadian rhythm (your sleep-wake cycle) and throw you off for a few days, she says.

How to fix it: At baseline, the solution is simply to get more sleep. But sometimes that’s easier said than done. You need to first figure out what the culprit is—stress? Netflix? Crappy sleep hygiene?—and then address it. If that still doesn't work, talk to your doctor about your options. You may need an intervention such as cognitive behavioral therapy to treat insomnia, for example.

Depression can cause a range of symptoms, and decreased energy or fatigue is definitely one of them, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). “Whenever I am screening a patient for depression, feelings of fatigue and loss of energy are one of the symptoms I always inquire about,” says Dr. Seawell.

These are the symptoms of depression to be familiar with, according to the NIMH.

Worth noting: Not everyone with depression experiences every symptom, per the NIMH. So, it’s entirely possible for you to feel tired on the regular and not even realize that it’s due to depression.

How to fix it: In this case, you need to address the underlying cause of your fatigue before you’ll feel better. Depression can be treated with psychotherapy, medication, or a combination of the two. If you suspect that your fatigue is linked to depression, though, it’s best to talk to your doctor about getting evaluated.

Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck that produces hormones that regulate how your body uses energy. When it doesn't produce enough thyroid hormone, it causes a condition known as hypothyroidism, which can mess with or slow down many of your body's functions, according to MedlinePlus.

“Thyroid hormones have receptors on essentially every organ of the human body and their deficiency can cause fatigue by excessively slowing the metabolic pathways,” explains Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: The treatment for hypothyroidism is taking medication to replace the hormone that your own thyroid can no longer make or create a sufficient amount of to keep your body functioning normally. Just know this: It may take a little while to feel better. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication until you reach the optimal level.

Just because you’re on the mend from, say, a virus doesn’t mean you should expect to bounce back energy-wise automatically. Recovery can take time. "A viral or bacterial infection can cause dehydration, generalized inflammation, and immense fatigue," says Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: First, give yourself time to recoup. Drink plenty of water and just take it easy, and you should feel less tired and more like yourself in a week or two.

Anemia is a condition in which your blood has fewer than normal red blood cells or hemoglobin, according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI). Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that helps red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. According to the NHLBI, if you have anemia, your body doesn't get enough oxygen-rich blood. So, if you have the condition, you can struggle with “fatigue and excessive tiredness,” says Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: It depends on the type of anemia you have. For some types of mild to moderate anemia, you may just need to add OTC or prescription iron supplements to your regimen. But your doctor may also suggest certain vitamins, IV therapy, or medicines that make your body produce more red blood cells, according to the NHLBI. You may also need to incorporate more iron-rich foods into your diet. Basically, you should see your doc for this one.

Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. In some people, gluten damages the small intestine and causes symptoms like bloating, diarrhea, constipation, gas, nausea, stomach pain, vomiting, and yep, fatigue, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK). That happens to people with celiac disease.

This condition can also cause long-term digestive issues that keep you from getting the nutrients you need and, in turn, cause ongoing fatigue.

How to fix it: Celiac disease can be tricky to diagnose, but after a physical exam, your doctor may recommend a blood test and an intestinal biopsy to check for inflammation in your small intestine. If you are confirmed to have celiac disease, you’ll need to avoid foods containing gluten in the future.

This is a less likely diagnosis, but it’s still worth mentioning. MS is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the brain and spinal cord, damaging the myelin, the covering of nerve fibers, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS).

Fatigue is a very common symptom in people with MS—about 80 percent of patients struggle with it, according to the NMSS. The fatigue can significantly interfere with a person’s ability to function, even if they feel good otherwise. It can result from treatable medication side effects or other factors.

How to fix it: Specific treatments can help people with MS manage fatigue, including occupational therapy to simplify tasks at home, physical therapy to learn energy-saving ways to walk and do other day-to-day tasks, a regular exercise program, sleep regulation, and psychological interventions, per the NMSS.

This is another one to add to the category of “unlikely but worth knowing.” Cancer-related fatigue is incredibly common: At least 80 percent of people diagnosed with the condition experience it, according to the American Cancer Society (ACS). While cancer treatments could be to blame, people with cancer can also feel wiped out just from the disease itself. It can disrupt almost all metabolic pathways and sabotage the body's mitochondrial energy, Dr. Khan explains.

How to fix it: First, don't freak out that you have a serious health issue. But know that getting a proper diagnosis is important and, from there, proper treatment is needed, which usually involves chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, or immunotherapy. The exact course depends on what type of cancer you have and how advanced it is. That's why seeing your doctor to rule it out is key if you haven't been able to shake your tiredness for a long time.

Here's the thing: Our body needs a range of nutrients and a certain number of calories per day to run at its normal capacity. Those numbers vary for everyone. "You need to not only make sure that you're providing yourself with a sufficient amount of calories per day to function, but also you need to be providing yourself with the appropriate nutrients," says Dr. Price.

If you don't, which can add to the fatigue, Dr. Price adds, even the smallest task feels monumental. You can also become constipated, says Dr. Price, which can contribute to the fatigue.

How to fix it: Eating a well-balanced diet and making sure that you’re eating enough fruits, vegetables, and proteins s essential to combatting fatigue, says Dr. Price. With the right nutrients, your body can create the energy you need to go about your day.

You’ve heard it before, but it’s true: Caffeine is a drug. Once your body gets accustomed to it, especially if you have coffee or soda every day, you become dependent on it. While it gives you a boost, caffeine also comes with highs and lows, and that can make you feel extremely tired, says Dr. Price. “Because you're burning calories when you have caffeine, you're moving at a faster pace, and you get to your peak of exhaustion much quicker,” she explains.

If you absolutely need coffee to get through your day, that should be a warning sign. "You should not have to have coffee in order to function, and something else is going on in your life that is causing you to be extremely fatigued," notes Dr. Price.

How to fix it: Switch up how you get your caffeine and start weaning yourself off of it. It'll take some adjustment, and you might get headaches at first, but once your body no longer depends on coffee, you'll feel a lot better.

While the medical world is still trying to figure out the long-term effects of COVID-19, we do know the toll the disease has on your body is that it makes you extremely exhausted, says Dr. Price. Your body tries to recuperate when you're infected—you lose your appetite, your muscles are extremely fatigued, and your body works in overdrive.

“Your body is doing the most to get you back to your normal self and to fight off COVID, so once you're done with it, you're not just going to bounce right back to yourself," says Dr. Price. “It's also been shown that the peak symptoms of COVID can sometimes be 14 days later. People must keep in mind this isn't a short illness. There are different and great severities of it."

Long COVID usually occurs two months after a person had COVID, says Dr. Price. If, two months after contracting the novel coronavirus, you’re still feeling worn out, it could be long COVID, she says.

How to fix it: The best way to protect yourself against COVID and the long-term complications is to get vaccinated and boosted and keep practicing good hygiene. If you suspect you have long COVID, visit your primary care provider and discuss your symptoms, Dr. Price advises. They can help you figure out your next steps.

Feeling tired once in a while is pretty normal—but experiencing constant fatigue isn’t. If you’re struggling, Dr. Khan recommends seeing your doctor. They’ll likely order several tests, including a physical exam and blood work, to figure out what, if anything, is happening.

"It's never too soon to go and talk to your doctor," says Dr. Price. What you thought might be minor, the doctor might look into more. "Or maybe you started googling things and, of course, Google will tell you you're dying, so talking to your doctor can give you relief and reassurance," Dr. Price adds.

The upside: the sooner you seek help, the sooner you can get answers—and get back to your rejuvenated and energetic self.

#5072. Tether Holds 150,000 Bitcoin, CEO Says—About 50,000 More Than Its Reserve Report Shows

Tether Holds 150,000 Bitcoin, CEO Says—About 50,000 More Than Its Reserve Report Shows

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said the stablecoin giant now holds around 150,000 Bitcoin, worth roughly $11.5 billion at current prices, a figure that exceeds what the company’s own reserve disclosures imply by some 50,000 coins.

“We have give or take 150,000 bitcoin ourselves. It’s not much, but it’s honest work,” Ardoino said during a keynote at the Plan ₿ Forum in Lugano, Switzerland, the city where Tether has run a Bitcoin and stablecoin adoption program since 2022.

The claim is notable because it doesn’t square neatly with the paper trail. Tether’s third-quarter reserve attestation, which covers the assets backing its USDT stablecoin, lists $8.37 billion of Bitcoin valued at $83,621 per coin, implying roughly 100,060 BTC.

That leaves about 50,000 coins, worth close to $3.8 billion, that its public filings do not yet account for. Ardoino did not say where the additional Bitcoin is held or when it was acquired, so his comment doesn’t indicate a fresh purchase of that size, and Tether has long maintained that its corporate Bitcoin investments sit separately from the reserves supporting USDT.

The stablecoin issuer has been accumulating Bitcoin for years. In May 2023, Tether said it would funnel up to 15% of its net realized operating profits into Bitcoin, and that it would custody the coins itself rather than rely on third-party custodians.

The strategy has been fueled by staggering profits: the company reported $1.5 billion in net operating profit in the third quarter alone, and it has posted billion-dollar quarterly profits throughout the year while its USDT supply has kept growing.

The broader reserve picture, as laid out in the Q3 report, shows $191.45 billion in assets against $183.50 billion in liabilities, leaving an excess cushion of $7.95 billion, nearly double the $4.11 billion buffer it reported in June. U.S. Treasury bills remain the bulk of reserves at about $132.4 billion.

The transparency gap is a sensitive subject for Tether, which has faced years of scrutiny over whether USDT is fully backed. The company began its first full financial audit with KPMG this year, a long-awaited step toward addressing those doubts.

Ardoino also used the Lugano stage to tout Tether’s scale, saying the company now serves more than 730 million users worldwide and is adding roughly 30 million wallets a quarter, as he pitched a suite of open-source technologies funded by its profits.

#5071. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeats Jon Husted, dealing a blow to crypto PAC Fairshake

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Earlier this year, Fairshake threw millions of dollars into the Ohio race, positioning itself against former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is taking back his spot in the Senate, leaving crypto political action committee Fairshake with the bag as he beats out incumbent Republican Jon Husted.

On Tuesday night, Brown defeated Husted in the race for Ohio's Senate seat, dealing a setback to Fairshake, a top crypto political action committee that committed tens of millions of dollars to keep Brown out of Washington.

Earlier this year, Fairshake threw $30 million into the Ohio race, positioning itself against Brown. The crypto PAC and the broader crypto industry played a significant role in the 2024 elections, spending millions to influence political outcomes.

This is not Fairshake's first time spending against Brown. He was previously the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, where he set the agenda for crypto and called for a crackdown on the use of cryptocurrency to fund terrorism and evade sanctions.

Then in 2024, Fairshake spent $12 million to back crypto-friendly Republican Bernie Moreno against Brown, defeating him. Since Democrats regained control of the Senate, Brown could become chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee, which has jurisdiction over digital assets and prediction markets, among other things. If he is chair, sources previously told The Block that Brown would be unlikely to introduce any crypto legislation.

Sen. Husted, who is endorsed by crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto, has voted yes for a few crypto bills, including the broad crypto legislation called the Clarity Act. Husted has an A rating from the group and gave Brown an F.

Other candidates backed by Stand With Crypto such as Democrat Chris Pappas in New Hampshire won their race.

Other pivotal Senate wins include Democratic Sens. Cory Booker and Mark Warner, both of whom have been a part of the negotiations for crypto legislation. Senate Democratic candidate in Texas, James Talarico, received an A rating from crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto for his previous pro-crypto statements and his vote to create a strategic bitcoin reserve in Texas. Talarico also won his race on Tuesday against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

#5070. On Wants You to Feel Your Softest Ride Yet

The Cloudsurfer 3 is built to make everyday runs feel smooth and effortless, even as the miles add up.

Just because you run doesn’t necessarily mean that you’re up on running shoe innovation. In recent years, there have been notable improvements in propulsion and efficiency, thanks to additions like carbon-fiber plates, smart sensors, and midsoles that promise high energy return. What’s more important than these buzzy words is: How do the shoes feel?

After all, you can have footwear designed by rocket scientists, but if you’re uncomfortable with every step, your run will be a slog, no matter the distance. You want your shoe to make the ride feel soft, which is why the On Cloudsurfer 3 stands out over so many others.

On running shoes have always been distinguished by their trademark hollow pods— the “clouds” that are specifically engineered to help create a softer underfoot experience and give the brand its unmistakable look. In the Cloudsurfer 3, On’s CloudTec Phase™ allows those pods to compress in sequence, helping absorb impact and create a smoother transition from heel to toe. This isn’t just another update to On’s running shoe line. With breakthrough Swiss engineering working beneath every step, the Cloudsurfer 3 delivers the brand’s softest ride yet.

An option for everyday and recovery runs as well as longer training sessions, the Cloudsurfer 3 combines CloudTec® Phase with On’s brand-new SurrealTM Superfoam. According to the brand’s internal testing, the pairing provides 15.5 percent deeper compression—and therefore more impact absorption—than the superfoam alone. The result is a softer landing that can help daily miles feel easier on the legs, particularly over long distances.

According to the same internal testing, the Cloudsurfer 3 is also predicted to deliver a 9.9 percent improvement in smooth-ride sensation. That figure reflects the way the reimagined CloudTec® Phase orientation enhances the rolling motion of the foot, helping each step flow more naturally into the next from landing to toe-off.

You’re also getting a newly engineered mesh upper in the Cloudsurfer 3, which provides a secure fit that adapts to your foot while still offering breathability and support. That breathability helps keep heat and moisture from building up, reducing the conditions that can lead to chafing, blisters, and hot spots.

Even the cushioning around the collar and tongue has been updated, so you get a cloud-like feel as soon as you slip them on. It doesn’t hurt that the Cloudsurfer 3 looks cool, too.

Together, these innovations give runners what they want from an everyday shoe: a natural feel, reliable performance, and lasting comfort. The result is a smoother ride, whether you’re going long or heading out for a quick training run.

That softer feel is a big deal, considering a 2025 study found that runners who perceived their shoes as more cushioned had a lower risk of running-related injury. When a shoe feels right, you’re less likely to think about every step—or adjust the way you’re moving to compensate for discomfort. That allows you to settle into your natural stride and focus on the run itself.

Enjoyment is a major factor, too. Wearing a shoe like the Cloudsurfer 3, with its focus on cushioning, responsiveness, and comfort, can be key to unlocking your best run yet—and enjoying yourself along the way. When that happens, even a hard run can feel softer, mile after mile.

#5069. 8 Best Hand Creams of 2026: 3-plus Years of Editor Testing and Reviews

From Joonbyrd to L’Occitane, here’s what formulas actually work.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ll be the first to admit it: I spend a copious amount of money on spa treatments and refining my at-home skincare routine. From my $78 Isdin sunscreen and Paula’s Choice Exfoliant to biweekly facials, my focus has always been on achieving clear, wrinkle-free skin without injections. But after chatting with double board-certified dermatologist Serena Mraz, MD, I realized that I’ve been neglecting my hands for far too long.

As a New Yorker, I take the subway several times a day for work, events, and to meet up with friends. I’m also a germaphobe and rely on hand sanitizer or harsh soap in office and restaurant bathrooms after riding the train. As a result, my hands are inevitably dry, dull, and rough. That's not exactly the look I’m going for as our beauty editor. It also doesn’t help that Dr. Mraz says cumulative sun damage, including dark spots and wrinkles, is one of the biggest culprits in showing my age. Wait, what do you mean my age didn’t pause during the pandemic? “Your skin records sun exposure like your car tallies mileage,” dermatologist Hadley King, MD, previously told me about how skincare changes in your 40s. “You can't turn back the odometer on your car, and you can't turn back sun damage from your skin."

Hand creams provide instant hydration and support the skin barrier, helping me achieve the baby-soft skin of my dreams. I’ve noticed that investing in my favorites lets me reapply less frequently and use a smaller amount of product, ultimately trimming my cost per use. It’s beauty math, ladies!

Creams, such as L'Occitane and Beau Domaine, are the thickest and most nourishing type of hand care products. Dr. Mraz is a fan of creams because they’re packed with more lipids than water, which helps deliver the best moisture. The downside is that they take longer to rub into your hands and across larger areas like your arms.

Ointments, such as Aquaphor and Vaseline, are versatile, fragrance-free moisturizers that relieve dryness without causing irritation, says dermatologist and clinical professor of dermatology Gary Goldenberg, MD. They’re made with petrolatum to keep your skin moist, which helps prevent wounds from drying out and forming a scab. These are especially useful when you have super cracked skin.

Lotions are thinner and more fluid than creams. Some are even runny, but don’t worry: the right lotions still restore moisture for instant relief and prevent dryness. Notably, our best overall pick—Joonbyrd Wonder·Land Hand Lotion—has a luxurious consistency that feels and smells like it belongs in a spa. It’s so enjoyable, I use it all over my body and notice instant hydration without leaving residue on my clothes.

The dermatologists I consulted recommend moisturizing ingredients glycerin, shea butter, and cocoa butter—they can be found in many of our suggestions, like Aquaphor and Juara.

Hyaluronic acid is another standout that acts as a moisture magnet, holding up to 1,000 times its weight in water. It’s so epic that dermatologists recently told me you can even use hyaluronic acid on your hair and scalp.

As our fragrance-obsessed beauty editor, I also factored in the scent profiles. While all of these hand creams smell good, I also highlighted the key notes that make each one stand out. Homecourt's five impressive aromas—ranging from roses to citrus and aromatic—and Juara's Bali-inspired coconut blend are some of my favorites. If scents aren’t your thing, opt for Nécessaire. What it lacks in aroma, it makes up for in skin-nourishing and soothing ingredients, including ceramides and niacinamide.

To kick off this evaluation process, I went directly to medical experts about their no-fail hand creams.

Our team has been writing about hand creams since 2023. As our beauty editor, I refined our testing methodologies for 2026 to help you avoid buyer's remorse.

I opened the testing pool to 16 hand creams, but only eight were worth the hype. So how did I select them? In addition to ensuring these picks align with dermatological guidance, I compared 2026 launches (Joonbyrd) with reliable heavy-hitters, like L’Occitane and CeraVe. I also rummaged through the Women’s Health beauty closet and slathered on these hand creams. I started with my hands and explored how they work on different parts of my body, like my rough knees, elbows, and feet.

To narrow the list further, I used these hand creams twice daily for five months. I adored our best overall pick so much that I used it for an entire month straight before even writing this story because it’s genuinely that good.

I didn’t want the hand cream application to feel like a mundane process. To help you actually finish your next tube of hand cream, I evaluated each contender’s sensory experience. These factors included fragrance, texture, absorption time, finish, and if they left any residue on my gloves and tech.

Lastly, I considered each item’s cost relative to its product size and quality of ingredients and effectiveness. This final list includes a mix of affordable, mid-range, and splurge-worthy picks that provide varying levels of hydration and other cosmetic-enhancing benefits like lightening age spots.

Ready to make dry hands a thing of the past? Look no further than these eight expert-approved hand creams worthy of a spot in your routine.

As our beauty editor, I’m constantly searching for the next big thing. My new undisputed no. 1 hand cream hails from the U.K. and it quickly became my all-time favorite recommendation. Joonbyrd was developed by dermatologist Alexis Granite, MD, who is certified in America and the U.K. Given her elite medical background—Dr. Granite was a clinical instructor at New York-Presbyterian/Weill-Cornell—my expectations for her line were high.

Joonbyrd offers two hand care products: the featured Wonder·Land Hand Lotion and the Confetti Sky Hand Treatment. TBH, the latter is compact and more travel-friendly, but I genuinely love the Hand Lotion so much that I apply it to my body. I initially tested it for one month straight before comparing it to other picks. (More on that shortly!) Since then, I’ve been reaching for it almost daily for a year. It offers long-lasting hydration and skin barrier support. Joonbyrd is so effective at leaving my skin softer and more supple that even acquaintances have noticed how soft my hands feel.

To ensure others received a fair assessment during the second month of my testing process, I evaluated how Joonbyrd compared with other options.

Joonbyrd wins over the French staple, as it’s lighter and features a modern formula that strengthens the skin barrier. L’Occitane remains a beauty classic, but if you want something new that you can apply all over your body, opt for Joonbyrd.

Go with the latter if you’re a price-conscious shopper or just super sensitive to scents. Hey, it happens to me during the spring and summer, so I totally get it! Joonbyrd is luxurious—the pretty packaging elevates my vanity setup, and the green, textured exterior helps prevent it from rolling off my table.

Joonbyrd is a non-sticky lotion that absorbs quickly, leaving no pesky residue on my belongings. It’s your best bet when your hands require barrier support and nourishment. On the flip side, Aquaphor feels heavy compared to Joonbyrd’s formulation, but not as greasy as Vaseline. (More on that soon—promise!)

Here’s where things get tougher. HomeCourt offers an aspirational, Insta-famous brand vibe, but with hydrating ingredients that enhance my skin. But if I could only own one hand cream, I’d opt for Joonbyrd since it’s cosmetically elegant and effective. FWIW, HomeCourt makes a body care collection if you prefer. I’m also so obsessed with the 2026 Skincare Award-winning Exfoliating Hand Soap.

Both hand creams provide ample skin-replenishing goodness. While the fragrance-free Nécessaire Hand Cream is helpful for anyone with a sensitive nose and skin, I do miss having access to the line’s signature scents at my disposal.

Overall, Joonbyrd is the best hand cream to beat in 2026. I’ll continue using this nourishing lotion for its standout ingredients, luxurious feeling, and impressive short- and long-term performance. Plus, the packaging is pretty and adds a fun, feminine touch to my vanity. The container has a nice weight and features a lightly cushioned textured green exterior to help prevent accidental slippage.

So what makes it so iconic? L’Occitane is made with gentle, effective ingredients, such as 20 percent organic shea butter, glycerin, and skin-plumping omegas. The consistency is thick enough to keep my hands hydrated overnight, yet it absorbs relatively fast enough that it won't leave a trail on my keyboard.Before I wrote about beauty for nine years, I was a tad excessive with products. Aquaphor and Vaseline are similar drugstore staples—they both use petroleum to lock in moisture and repair the skin barrier. But Aquaphor takes the edge since it contains humectants to draw water to the skin for additional hydration, dermatologist Alicia Zalka, MD, previously told us. It’s made with a mineral oil called paraffinum liquidum and a wax called ceresin. There’s also soothing bisabolol, and a blend of hydrating glycerin, lanolin, and panthenol.

Since Aquaphor contains more ingredients than Vaseline, it hits the moisturizing trifecta by acting as an occlusive (a thick, protective layer), emollient (trapping moisture in the skin), and humectant (drawing in hydration). It’s not the most exciting product on this list, but it’s certainly effective and ideal for someone who prefers a no-frills routine. Aquaphor also creates a protective barrier between your skin and the elements during high-altitude skiing and snowboarding sessions.

Given its TSA-friendly size, it’s also a must-have during my in-flight beauty routine.While the upfront cost is a bit jarring, Beau Domaine’s dual-action formula justifies the cost. Deal with itchy, scaly hands? You’ll need something offering more intensive hydration without compromising on gentle components. Dr. Ruth recommends this hand cream and says it’s a popular pick among her patients with eczema.

Though Juara doesn't make any specific eczema safety certifications, Dr. Ruth doesn’t mind it for her patients with that skin condition. TBH, my eczema flares up during the winter and seasonal transitions, but this nourishing cream hasn’t caused any sensitivity issues.

Most know Lait-Crème Concentré as a face moisturizer and makeup primer—it leaves my skin dewy even after using retinol—but it functions six ways, including as a hand cream. Wait, what? Mhmmm, I apply a small pea-sized amount of Lait-Crème Concentré to hydrate my hands without feeling greasy or sticky. Chock-full of shea butter and soothing aloe vera, my hands look visibly hydrated and luminous. I rub it into my hands and get back to typing on my laptop or phone within a minute.

With holiday travel coming up, carry-on space is limited and valuable. Think of Lait-Crème Concentré as the Swiss Army knife of skincare. It works as a moisturizing face mask, after-sun treatment, shaving cream, and cleansing milk—yup, just add a little water for a hydrating wash. Still, at just $19 for an icon from the French pharmacy, you can’t go wrong, especially since you won’t deal with VAT refunds at CDG Airport in Paris.

#5068. Influencers Are Doing ‘Olive Oil Shots.’ We Asked 4 Experts If That’s a Good Idea—and They All Basically Said the Same Thing.

The truth about the supposed health practice—revealed.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

SO OLIVE OIL shots are a thing again. Remember in the mid- to late-2010s, when people were knocking back all manner of liquids, including apple cider vinegar, juiced ginger, pulverized turmeric, and extra virgin olive oil? Well, social media influencers have brought back at least the last one, with Bryan Johnson doing “evo” shots and Steven Gundry, MD, recommending a daily dose of the stuff. (Also, both those guys sell their own olive oil. Just saying.)

The supposed benefits of shooting olive range from the more generalized “more energy” to more specific ones, like protecting your cardiovascular system from disease.

Influencers usually back up these claims by citing scientific research on the benefits of adding olive oil to your daily diet. But do the benefits extend to doing shots of olive oil?

“Olive oil is great for heart health and contains beneficial polyphenols, but you don't need to take it as a shot. You get the same benefits by just including it in your meals, and it's generally much more enjoyable that way. But if you want to take it as a shot, there's no harm in that. It's just not superior to including olive oil in your diet in regular ways. You know, with food.”

“I'm a fan of California Olive Ranch 100% California Extra Virgin Olive Oil For Everyday. It's high quality, reasonably affordable (for evoo), and widely available. I use it to saute veggies, roast tubers and veggies, and drizzle on various things.”

“I'm a bigger fan of eating a few shots of olive oil with sauteed veggies or I pour it on my food. But a shot is fine I guess. People like to do it in the longevity scene to invoke ancient Greeks doing shots of ‘liquid gold.’”

“I am an affiliate of the Fresh Pressed Olive Oil Club, which I reallly love. I've not had lots of fancy, fresh olive oils from around the world before and now I have. I like seeing and tasting the diversity. I use a 1-liter glass bottle of EVOO, usually Braggs or Whole Food Organic. I try to go through two to three of these a month for our house of four.”

“I wouldn’t suggest shots of olive oil for any reason. All that’s happening here is that you’re adding a concentrated source of calories and fat to your diet. There are no documented benefits of doing this for the average person, and it can cause weight gain if the oil shots are taken in addition to someone’s current diet. This can ultimately cause health problems.”

“I don’t really have a fave oil. I use brands that have a seal of origin in them to ensure their purity.”

“While olive oil is full of beneficial compounds that may support heart health and longevity, shooting it isn't necessary. Heating olive oil may degrade some beneficial polyphenols, but using it as a salad dressing, sauce, or finishing oil for roasted veggies provides the same benefits, plus enhanced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and carotenoids.”

“Extra-virgin olive oil can have such a range of flavors. I love San Giuliano Coastal Harvest Olive Oil. It's cold-pressed, which helps preserve more nutrients and polyphenols, and has a really nice, peppery flavor. While I don't take shots of it, I regularly use it in dressings and over veggies.”

Paul Kita is a Deputy Editor at Men's Health, where he has covered food, cooking, nutrition, supplements, grooming, tech, travel, and fatherhood at the brand for more than 15 years. He is also the author of two Men's Health cookbooks, Guy Gourmet and A Man, A Pan, A Plan, and the winner of a James Beard Award.

#5067. French bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa exploited for over $133 million, ZachXBT says

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

ZachXBT said he has a 'high degree of confidence' that the attacker is not associated with North Korea's Lazarus Group.

Onchain investigator ZachXBT has identified French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa as the alleged victim of a theft estimated at more than $133 million.

ZachXBT first reported on Nov. 2 that an unnamed EU entity had lost over $106 million from multiple centralized exchange accounts the previous day, with funds withdrawn as USDC and USDT.

A day later, he raised the total stolen amount to above $133 million after tracing an additional $27 million in withdrawals, some of which occurred after his initial disclosure. He speculated that a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and currently being covered up.

On the evening of Nov. 3, he stated that the institution is allegedly Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a French bank with approximately $235 billion in assets. He noted that the attack spanned multiple days and suggested the actual losses could be higher when accounting for possible over-the-counter activity.

"Over the past 24 hours the illicit actor has been aggressively swapping USDC for ETH, transferring to instant exchanges (WellWallet, Kyrrex, etc), converting to XMR via Wagyu, and bridging across multiple chains," ZachXBT wrote in his Nov. 2 message in his Telegram group, adding that he has a "high degree of confidence" that the attacker is not associated with North Korea's Lazarus Group.

He has criticized the institution for allegedly allowing more than $30 million to be laundered, noting that proper incident disclosure to EU law enforcement could have frozen the funds.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has not issued any public statement confirming or denying the incident. The Block has reached out to the bank but has not heard back. The claims remain based on ZachXBT's own analysis and have not been independently verified by the bank or authorities.

The bank has more than 5.6 million customers, with total assets of 211.5 billion euros (around $237 billion).

#5066. Ethereum dev targets 2028 for quantum resistance, a year early

Ethereum researcher Justin Drake said it is their “hope” that Ethereum will achieve its post-quantum and post-AI transition by December 2028.

Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake is targeting December 2028 to complete Ethereum’s post-quantum and post-AI transition, a year earlier than the foundation’s previously announced quantum-resistance deadline.

Speaking at Devcon 8 in Mumbai on Tuesday, Drake outlined the accelerated timeline. “Our hope is that by December 2028 we’ll be able to wrap up the full post-quantum and post-AI transition,” Drake said, adding that developers have 24 months to deliver three additional network upgrades.

The Ethereum Foundation’s September roadmap established December 2029 as its deadline for achieving quantum resistance across Ethereum’s execution, consensus and data layers.

Drake’s remarks signal a more ambitious timeline but do not formally replace the foundation’s existing roadmap, which is scheduled for reassessment in January 2027.

In August, Drake outlined plans for production-ready leanVM technology in 2027, followed by post-quantum deployments across Ethereum’s three layers in 2028.

The timeline has drawn scrutiny from other blockchain developers. In October, Starknet’s community backed research into becoming an independent post-quantum layer-1 network.

StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson previously told Cointelegraph that Ethereum’s 2029 target was “too late,” warning that deadlines could slip.

#5065. OpenAI Wants to Rebrand AI Data Centers, Use Them to 'Protect the Grid'

OpenAI Wants to Rebrand AI Data Centers, Use Them to 'Protect the Grid'

OpenAI wants its massive AI data centers to help keep the lights on when electricity grids come under pressure. And, apparently, it would also prefer that people stop calling them AI data centers.

The ChatGPT developer announced its Grid Protectors Program on Monday, a national initiative designed to let future AI facilities reduce electricity consumption during emergencies and periods of high demand, potentially lowering costs for other customers.

Under the plan, OpenAI would coordinate with utility companies to determine how much electricity its facilities could temporarily stop using, how quickly they could respond, and for how long. The company is also exploring on-site batteries and power generation to help manage demand.

“Families and small businesses should not be asked to subsidize a compute campus’s electricity needs,” OpenAI said in its announcement.

The program addresses one of the biggest complaints surrounding the AI infrastructure boom: companies are building increasingly power-hungry facilities while residents worry about paying higher—and water—electricity bills to support them.

OpenAI is using a planned facility in Effingham County, Georgia, as its first example. The company has signed a 25-year agreement with Georgia Power covering approximately 3,200 megawatts of electricity demand, with up to 1,000 megawatts available for temporary reductions during periods of high demand.

Under the approved agreement, OpenAI must cover the full infrastructure costs required to serve its facility, rather than passing those expenses on to existing customers.

Georgia Power also projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029, equivalent to at least $15 per month for a typical residential customer. However, those estimates cover the utility's broader portfolio of large electricity customers and expected growth, not just OpenAI's project.

The Georgia facility is still under development, and the savings remain projections. OpenAI has not yet disclosed binding demand-reduction commitments for other facilities under its national program.

OpenAI's electricity initiative also arrives after reports of a massive PR campaign to change what people call the facilities in the first place to erase from collective memory the negative sentiment towards AI data centers.

According to Axios, OpenAI is preparing a post-midterm policy and PR campaign that includes rebranding data centers as "AI compute campuses," an effort to make the infrastructure sound more appealing to communities, effectively trying to solve a problem by changing the problem’s name.

The company has already started using the terminology. Its Grid Protectors announcement repeatedly refers to future facilities as "compute campuses," although it occasionally uses the more familiar term "data centers."

An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the naming strategy to Business Insider, arguing that the term better reflects the facilities' broader role in computing, energy infrastructure, and skilled employment.

The reported rebranding comes as opposition to AI infrastructure projects has become a political issue across the United States. Pennsylvania introduced new restrictions on large data centers in August, including provisions designed to protect residents from higher electricity costs. Other states are following.

OpenAI and six other major technology companies also signed a White House pledge in March to pay for the electricity and grid upgrades their AI projects require.

The new program goes further by proposing that AI facilities could become useful to utilities rather than simply adding pressure to their systems. But the national framework is still largely an ambition, with individual agreements to be negotiated.

OpenAI's Georgia project will provide an early test of that approach. Electricity delivery to the planned 3.2-gigawatt facility is scheduled to begin in 2028 and expand in phases through 2032.

#5064. I Tried Two New Therabody Devices. Now I Have a Tension-Melting Routine

Combining heat, massage, and targeted percussive therapy helps me decompress from the day.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I carry my stress in my shoulders and my neck. I always have. It’s the last quarter of the year, when my job responsibilities tend to ramp up, and my family responsibilities have increased this year, too. Recently, I started running regularly again to help find some me-time, but instead of releasing tension, the activity has left my traps and neck stiff. No amount of meditation or yoga is releasing these burdens that have nested into my shoulders, upper back, and neck.

Luckily, Therabody needed someone to try its newest massagers: ThermNeck & Upper Back and ThermFace Massage. I was their girl. Full disclosure: I’m a Theragun fan. It’s been helping me recover from workouts and race training for years. Products that target my stress zone sounded promising—and much-needed. I love my Theragun, but it can be unwieldy when I try to reach those areas myself. So I began working the two Therabody massagers into my after-work wellness routine. Here’s how it went.

First, I started with ThermFace Massage. When I initially heard about it, I wasn’t sure what to expect—or whether I’d like it. I live with migraine, so I was cautious about the prospect of vibration around my head.

ThermFace Massage may look just like a smaller Theragun, but it isn’t. It’s Therabody’s first heated percussive massage device specifically engineered to handle the delicate muscles of the face, jaw, and neck. It has 5-millimeter amplitude, three speeds, three heat levels, and four specialized attachments—Heat, Cone, Dampener, and Wedge—that allows you to customize the experience. And unlike the Theragun, ThermFace Massage has a 45-degree ergonomic shape that makes it easier to navigate all contours of the jaw, face, and neck.

The first time I used it, I chose the softest attachment and started on the right side of my neck. I turned it on at the lowest speed and moved slowly, paying close attention to how my body responded. The sensation was targeted but not aggressive. Once I felt comfortable, I guided it along the muscles of my jaw, where I hadn’t fully realized I was holding tension.

That became my first lesson: Stress doesn’t always announce itself. Sometimes it shows up as a clenched jaw during a difficult email, a tight face at the end of a long day, or stiffness that seems to travel from the jaw into the neck.

Next, I tested the heat attachment. ThermFace Massage offers three temperature settings ranging from 40°C to 55°C. This allowed me start conservatively rather than jump straight to the warmest option, which has since become my favorite setting. The combination of adjustable heat and focused percussion made the routine feel purposeful: I’m taking care of my overlooked, overworked muscles.

Because I live with migraine, I remain deliberate about where and how I use the device, but I haven’t experienced an increase in episodes while using ThermFace Massage. Anyone managing a health condition should check with a medical professional before introducing a new device into their routine, as I did before I started this trial.

Next came the ThermNeck & Upper Back, a cordless wearable designed to target the neck, trapezius muscles, and upper back. If ThermFace Massage helped me notice how much tension I carried around my jaw, ThermNeck & Upper Back went straight to the place where I already knew my stress lived.

It combines five complementary therapies in one device: kneading massage, heat, far-infrared, near-infrared LED light, and Theragun percussive therapy. Two built-in Theraguns are positioned over the trapezius muscles (located in the upper back), and the device includes three percussive speeds, three kneading patterns, and three heat levels.

I slipped it over my shoulders while seated on my sofa and used the adjustable strap to fine-tune the placement and pressure. It’s wearable, but not completely hands-free; resting my hands in the straps allowed me to control how firmly the device sat against my muscles.

That adjustability mattered. After a run, I may want a different intensity than I do after eight hours at my computer. Some evenings, I’m looking for targeted percussion. On others, soothing heat and kneading massage are more appealing. Depending on what my body needs on a given day, I can tailor my time with the device.

ThermNeck & Upper Back should be used while seated or standing, not while lying down. I found sitting on the sofa to be the ideal setup—comfortable enough to decompress, but upright enough to keep the device properly positioned.

Now when I get home from work, I change into comfy clothes, make dinner for my family, then slip on ThermNeck & Upper Body and watch television while the device kneads away the stress of the day that has built up in my neck and upper back. Five minutes is all it takes to transition from responsibility mode to evening mode, making me more relaxed and calm for the time that means the most to me: family time.

The hour before bed, I brush my teeth, wash my face, use my TheraFace Mask Glo (told you I was a Therabody fan), then retire to my bed. There, I use the ThermFace Massage (usually the Heat attachment) to massage my jaw and neck for a couple of minutes on each side, followed by reading and then sleep.

While none of the devices will erase my deadlines or family obligations, they do help with my running-related stiffness and ease the tension in the places where those pressures land. This routine has also created a better awareness around my head, neck, and shoulders: Am I clenching my jaw? Are my shoulders creeping toward my ears? Have I moved away from my screen recently?

Meditation and yoga still have a place in my life. But sometimes my stress feels less like a thought I can breathe through and more like a knot sitting directly on top of my shoulders. This new routine allows me to use targeted heat and massage to help loosen that knot with a few intentional minutes at the end of the day.

#5063. Morgan Stanley among first banks to tokenize US equities, Treasurys through DTCC’s service

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

The bank is among the first to use DTCC's new tokenization service as it separately prepares to support tokenized equities in Q1 2027.

Morgan Stanley has begun using the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation's new tokenization infrastructure to tokenize real-world assets, joining a group of financial institutions that accessed the service after its launch last week.

The bank said it has tokenized U.S. equities and Treasurys through the service, making it among the first to do so, according to an X post.

"The hands-on experience of integrating tokenized securities with established market infrastructure will inform the continued development of the firm's digital asset capabilities as the market evolves," said Amy Oldenburg, Morgan Stanley's head of digital assets strategy.

DTC, DTCC's depository subsidiary, which holds $114 trillion in assets under custody, signed 20 participants to access the service at launch, including Bank of America, Barclays, and BNP Paribas. Citi, Fidelity Investments, JPMorgan, State Street, and UBS were also listed, with plans to onboard future users on a rolling basis put in place.

DTCC said at the time the service was developed with input from more than 150 firms and initially supported Canton and its private Besu network.

The development comes as Morgan Stanley expects to support tokenized equities on its alternative trading system in the first quarter of 2027, later than its previous H2 2026 target. Oldenburg told The Block last month that the bank was building the necessary infrastructure for the initiative.

Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley is not alone in the tokenization race. The New York Stock Exchange and its parent, Intercontinental Exchange, are also advancing plans for a tokenized trading platform. Broadridge, Computershare, Equiniti, and Superstate have signed agreements to serve as transfer agents.

#5062. The 16 Best Men's Clothing Brands in 2026, According to Style Editors

From the OG classics to newcomer labels you need to know.

AS MEN’S HEALTH EDITORS, we give guys tools they need to level up their lives, and that includes your wardrobe. Enter: The best men's clothing brands for men, a shortlist of labels that deliver on style and function for every vibe and occasion. Whether you’re a seasoned fashion maven or just dipping your toes into the menswear game, having a solid rotation of duds you can rely on is key to looking sharp without overthinking it. Huckberry's in-house label delivers a rugged, workwear-inspired vibe, made with utility and style in mind. If you’re a busy body and constantly on the move, you can find a number of items to support your active lifestyle. As for casual outings, Mack Weldon has you covered in that area, too. Abercrombie used to be one of those mall-favorites back in the day, but the brand has since revamped its all-American cool–think easygoing duds, with a hint of vintage flair. Its range of versatile, premium-feeling designs are mostly laid-back and look great on guys of all ages. These threads work perfectly in casual environments where you want to look put-together but leave the high maintenance at home. At its core, the brand is all about comfort that doesn’t sacrifice style.

Whether you’re attending a music festival, cruising downtown with friends, or hitting up a weekend bonfire, you can find pieces that transition from day to night, making sure you’re always on point—no matter the occasion. Abercrombie specializes in those casual staples that you need in rotation such as cozy hoodies, sleek vegan leather jackets, perfectly worn-in t-shirts, and several types of denim cuts. When it comes to the latter, the 90s Straight Jean has been a huge hit, offering a wide selection of washes, plenty of stretch, and retro charm.
