Instead of sticking with small, medium, and large sizes, the brand’s assortment of pants features over 12 different waist sizes, plus a range of inseams and fits including athletic, slim taper, and straight. This means you’re guaranteed to find the perfect pair. In tandem with the selection of pants, the shirts come in a series of fits, too.

Aside from killer chinos, the vast inventory consists of golf gear, suits and blazers, swim trunks, and outerwear. In fact, it was the relaxed cut of The Harrington Jacket that resonated with us, which layers easily over all kinds of tops. All things considered, if you need new attire for the beach, the links, the office, or the weekend, it’s all here.

If you've never heard of Buck Mason, think of this LA-based brand as a one-stop-shop for guys who want to look put-together but not pretentious. Instead of chasing trends, the label is set on offering a refined take on everyday essentials, blending American style with modern tailoring and quality craftsmanship. In other words, its expertise lies in paying attention to the details: Taking into account fabric, fit, and function. After all, the brand acquired an American knitting mill to ensure its gear stays authentically made in the USA. As a result, this men’s clothing brand’s designs are about that understated style with classic silhouettes and muted color palettes, mixed with a twist of laid-back California vibes.

Falling in line with those aesthetics is its best-selling, signature Felted Chore Coat—simple at first glance, but crafted with purpose. We love that it's tailored with a slimmer cut through the arms for a sharper silhouette, while the roomier torso leaves space for layering. Plus, the felted merino wool allows you to capitalize on warmth, breathability, and softness without bulk.

In general, Buck Mason’s pieces work in a variety of settings—be it a dinner date, food festival, or Broadway show. Among its collection of garments is high-quality jeans, t-shirts and henleys, button-down shirts and lightweight jackets.

Todd Snyder is known for modernizing classic American menswear with tailored fits, top-of-the-line fabrics, and subtle yet stylish updates. The brand blends timeless silhouettes with contemporary details, often playing with rich textures and unique color palettes. While Todd Snyder is not exactly budget-friendly, the slew of suede jackets, wool coats, and refined suiting will let you channel the best A-listers in the game. In fact, its vintage-inspired sweaters and outerwear have even graced the likes of Chris Evans and Ryan Reynolds.

An undeniable standout is the Italian Suede Snap Dylan Jacket that’s structured enough to look sharp but accommodate easy layering. The trucker-style cut is crafted from buttery-soft calf suede, which not only gives luxury feels but also ages beautifully over time.

Another one of Todd Snyder's biggest strengths is its collaborations, from Timex watches to New Balance sneakers and Champion heritage sweatpants. These partnerships add a level of flair that few brands are able to mimic. Overall, TS expertly delivers high-quality, long-lasting staples that work for guys who want to look put-together without trying too hard.

Everlane is a men's clothing brand that follows its own path. It's really big on creating eco-conscious, classic clothes that will cycle through your ever-evolving wardrobe for years to come. Think authentic denim and minimal organic cotton tees priced so well that you won't have any other option than to stock up on multiple pairs and colorways.

If you're looking to stay cozy through the last stretch of winter, Everlane's got a whole Cashmere Shop filled with ultra-soft sweaters to keep you warm without overheating. The brand’s assortment also makes it easy to transition from the office to happy hour with its monochromatic shirting—from oxford shirts to shackets such as the versatile Heavyweight Overshirt—that has that just-right fit that's neither too slim nor too boxy.

Perhaps best known in the zeitgeist for its finance bro vests, Patagonia is in fact the leading outdoor apparel brand that makes clothes with adventures and extreme climates in mind. It has tons of hiking-inspired basics to anchor a stylish and functional closet. For starters, The Nano Puff Jacket is the gold standard of puffer jackets—light, warm, and endlessly versatile—ideal for street and trail wear. Not to mention, it's a warrior in all kinds of weather, thanks to the windproof and water-repellent exterior.

Its fleece layers are legendary, too. Take the Better Sweater Fleece Jacket, which is cozy, durable, and polished enough to wear just about anywhere. This silhouette is thicker than a standard fleece, but the regular fit allows you to layer effortlessly. In terms of style, you can wear it for weekend hikes or the nearest coffee shop for your daily pick-me-up.

This stalwart label has been in the game for ages and still gets it right—serving up sleek clothing for men, which embodies "quiet luxury" energy, minus the high-roller price tag. When it comes to styling Banana Republic, picture yourself nailing every look—from acing that morning meeting in a crisp dress shirt and tailored chinos, to seamlessly transitioning into dinner at a swanky bistro with a smart blazer.

The brand’s offerings are built for real life, so whether you’re powering through a busy workday, networking at after-hours events, or catching up with friends over drinks on the weekend, there’s something to fit the bill. Banana Republic specializes in dressier, well-cut staples: Sharp button-downs, versatile trousers, structured blazers, and quality knitwear that feels as good as it looks. But make no mistake, Banana Republic also plays with casual attire too. For example, the Ribbed Cotton Henley T-Shirt has that relaxed feel, which is great for those off-duty days when you’re picking up lunch or taking a laid-back stroll in the park.

Alex Mill’s been around for over a decade, carving out a reputation we’d describe as “Normcore classic.” In other words, the brand hits it on the nail when it comes to everyday basics—think slub tees that serve as the ultimate wardrobe workhorses, slightly cropped jeans that pair with any top, and washed chore coats that add dimension to any look. It’s all about minimal fuss, modern sensibility, and letting the pieces become more character-rich with every wear.

These garments really come into their own in spots like creative offices, co-working spaces, or that favorite local cafe—places where you want to look put-together without trying too hard. They’re perfect for laid-back brunches, art gallery openings, or casual dinner dates. Without seeming overdone, these staples can easily elevate your everyday style. Take the Garment Dyed Chore Jacket in Canvas, for instance: It's super low-key—not too in your face, yet still has that unique twist that any artist or designer would appreciate.

The Japanese brand helped redefine what great wardrobe essentials should feel like: clean, well-made, and affordable without ever looking cheap. Its lineup is built around minimal design and great-for-the-price fabrics (think Heattech thermals, a heat-retaining base layer designed to trap warmth without bulk, or Ultra Light Down, Uniqlo’s featherweight yet surprisingly warm down insulation), offering pieces that work across seasons—from crisp tees and chinos to cozy sweaters and functional outerwear that earns its closet space.

What makes Uniqlo a go-to is its ability to effortlessly fit into everyday life. These are clothes you grab on busy workdays, for travel, or just when you want to get dressed without overthinking it. Whether you’re layering thermals under a jacket for winter or reaching for a casual linen in the summer, Uniqlo’s pieces are the building blocks that make everything else in your wardrobe work better.

J.Crew is one of those heritage American labels that you often circle back to because it just gets the classics right. The brand is known for its preppy-meets-laid-back aesthetic, offering staples like blazers, button-downs, chinos, knitwear, and polos that feel polished but never stuffy.These are the kinds of pieces that carry you through a full day from the office to post-work drinks without needing an outfit change. If your style lives somewhere between casual and pulled-together, J.Crew makes it easy to look sharp in a way that feels chill and approachable at the same time.

Cos is the more elevated sibling to H&M—part of the same family, but built around higher-quality fabrics and more refined construction. Rather than chasing trends, Cos invests in premium wool blends, heavyweight cottons, and structured tailoring, which its pieces cost a bit more than its sister brand, but also hold their shape and look polished far longer. You’re paying for better fabric, cleaner finishing, and silhouettes that don’t feel disposable. Its lineup includes sharp wool overcoats, crisp poplin button-downs, substantial merino knits, and tailored trousers with a proper drape—all in shades like black, navy, charcoal, or stone. These clothes can transition from the office to a fancy dinner to speakeasy nightcap situation. Essentially, this is where you go for something a step above fast fashion minus the designer price tag.

Alo may have started as an active brand, but it’s evolved into a full-on lifestyle label that blends workout clothes with fits that you’d wear outside the gym. From moisture-wicking workout tees and sleek tanks to comfortable hoodies and joggers that look good in public, these are the pieces you throw on for a morning session, keep on for errands, travel days, or a casual lunch, and still feel clean.

Tailored cargo trousers, straight-leg Velour pants, and track pants with clean hems and minimal branding can pass at the office, while the carpenter-style bottoms and relaxed cargos feel polished enough for dinner plans. Up top, Alo’s bombers, pullover sweatshirts, and shackets are structured, not slouchy or logo-heavy, making them easy substitutes for a crewneck, knit, or light jacket.

If your uniform leans athletic but put-together, without looking like you just walked out of a sweat-drenched Barry’s class, Alo makes it easy to never feel under- or overdressed. One note: most of its clothing runs big, so be sure to size down for a closer fit, unless you prefer a looser cut.

Madewell established its reputation on solid denim, and that foundation still shows, but over the years the brand has evolved beyond jeans. Over the past few years, it’s quietly strengthened its menswear roster, offering easy essentials like soft tees, cozy knits, overshirts, and brushed flannels that layer cleanly without bunching. The overall vibe at Madewell is relaxed but put-together. These clothes are made for weekends, casual dinners, and low-key nights at a bar or speakeasy. They feel broken-in from day one but still read sharp. If your uniform starts with great denim and goes from there, Madewell is an excellent place to begin.

Few brands have done more to define American prep than Tommy Hilfiger. From rugby shirts and flag sweaters to chinos, polos, and lightweight outerwear, the label consistently delivers timeless staples that feel both classic and current. What keeps Tommy relevant, though, is its knack for evolving the formula through smart collaborations and fresh takes on heritage style. Recent partnerships, including its ongoing work with the U.S. SailGP Team, prove the brand still knows how to make prep feel cool for a new generation.

A polished but relaxed approach to office dressing that’s also suitable for after-work drinks—think chinos, dress shirts, knit polos, and unstructured blazers. Brands such as Bonobos, Alex Mill, and Banana Republic have this kind of style down pat.

If you have plans to attend a black-tie event, gala, wedding, or simply want to look extra sharp, you’ve got to suit up. In this case, you’ll turn to structured blazers, tailored trousers, dress shirts, and dress shoes in classic colors like navy, gray, and black. Brands such as Bonobos, Todd Snyder, Banana Republic, and Buck Mason have suiting on lock.

From lightweight jackets to heavy-duty coats, outerwear is all about function and style. This includes bombers, leather jackets, shackets, parkas, and puffers perfect for transitional weather or full-on winter. Brands such as Flint and Tinder, Patagonia, and Alex Mill will have you geared up.

Clothing designed for movement but stylish enough for everyday wear. Think workout shirts, joggers, sweat-wicking polos, gym shorts, and sneakers that work for both gym sessions and casual outings. Brands like Alo and Patagonia offer a solid collection of these duds.

Easygoing staples like jeans, hoodies, henleys, sneakers, and flannels—perfect for relaxed weekends, brunch, or laid-back office days. Brands such as Abercrombie, J.Crew, Everlane, and Uniqlo deliver in this category.

When shopping for the best clothing brands for men, fit is everything. It dictates not only how comfortable you feel but also how your outfit communicates your personal style. Generally, men’s garments are broken down into four broad categories: Relaxed, Tailored, Classic, and Slim. You don’t have to stick to just one, but each serves a different aesthetic and function—let’s break it down.

Relaxed-fit clothing is all about comfort. It’s cut with extra room through the chest, waist, and legs, allowing for a looser, more laid-back silhouette. This is ideal if you’re looking for casual wear, streetwear, and workwear-inspired looks. Think boxy tees, oversized hoodies, wide-leg trousers, and unstructured outerwear. Patagonia tends to lean into this fit as its fleece jackets, outerwear, and casual basics are built for movement and outdoor adventure. Alex Mill focuses on casual staples with slightly relaxed, vintage-inspired cuts.

A tailored fit offers a balance between structure and comfort. It follows the body’s shape without clinging too tightly, creating a refined yet wearable look. This is your go-to fit for business casual, smart casual, and elevated everyday wear. Think tapered chinos, slightly structured blazers, and slim-but-not-skinny button-downs.

Slim fits are designed for a clean, modern silhouette. These clothes contour the body without excessive looseness, making them ideal for dressier looks, contemporary minimalism, or even athleisure. Key pieces include slim-fit jeans, fitted turtlenecks, and sharply cut blazers.

Classic fit is the middle ground between relaxed and tailored, giving you room to move without excess fabric. This is the fit you’ll find in traditional menswear, from business suits to heritage denim. It’s not baggy, but it’s also not hugging your body either.

Not all clothes are created equal, and neither are price tags. Some items are worth dropping some serious cash on, while others can be a rip-off. The key is knowing when to invest and when to save because a well-thought-out wardrobe isn’t about spending the most, it’s about getting the most value out of what you buy.

This is your fast-fashion and essentials tier—solid for trying new styles or grabbing wardrobe basics without overthinking. But here’s the catch: Cheap can often mean short-lived. For instance, a $10 tee from a fast-fashion retailer may look good today but will likely warp, fade, or pill after a few washes. That’s fine for trends like an oversized striped tee you might wear for a season, but when it comes to daily staples, spending a little more pays off. You’d be better off spending $58 on an Alex Mill slub tee that lasts for years and is worn 50-plus times, which equals less than $2 per wear.

This is where cost meets quality. You’re getting better fabrics, stronger construction, and brands that care about longevity. Think nicer denim, well-cut chinos, and quality knitwear—things you’ll actually wear often, so the investment makes sense.

This is where justifiable spending comes into play. A $500 Buck Mason suede jacket? Pricey up front, but wear it 50 times per season for five years, and suddenly, it’s $2 per wear—less than a daily coffee. The same goes for boots—drop $300+ on a well-made pair, and you won’t have to replace them for a decade. In this price range, you find premium outerwear, leather goods, boots, and everyday pieces.

At this level, you’re paying for craftsmanship, exclusivity, and long-term investment. A $1,300 leather jacket from Todd Snyder isn’t for everyone, but if you’re buying into history, durability, and premium construction, it’ll outlive you. Same with a properly tailored suit—if you wear it for major life events over decades, it’s an investment, not an expense.

To find the best men's clothing brands, our fashion and commerce teams, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, spent the last five years putting over 80 menswear brands through the wringer, wearing threads to sweaty gym sessions, breezy hikes, long workdays, formal cocktail events, and casual weekend outings. Whether it was testing a fleece in the cold, seeing if dress shirts hold up in marathon meetings, or figuring out if chinos had enough stretch for comfort during a long-haul flight, we made sure these brands actually delivered on function as well as style.

From there, we narrowed it down to 16 standout brands based on quality, fit, signature styles, type of garment, and value. No fast fashion, no fleeting trends, just well-made, great-fitting essentials that look sharp on any guy, hold up over time, and feel like a solid investment for our wardrobe. #5060. Judge Orders Bitcoin Wallet Returned to Family of Convicted Canadian Killer

Judge Orders Bitcoin Wallet Returned to Family of Convicted Canadian Killer

A Canadian judge has ordered that a laptop containing a Bitcoin wallet be returned to the family of William Sandeson, who is serving a life sentence for the 2015 murder of fellow university student Taylor Samson during a drugs deal, Global News reported.

Justice John Bodurtha of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court ruled on Tuesday that prosecutors had not proved the cryptocurrency was linked to the killing. Sandeson, who appeared virtually at the hearing in Halifax, had filed a motion in April seeking the return of personal items seized when police searched his apartment after his arrest in 2015.

"The Crown has not met its burden to demonstrate the cryptocurrency was used as part of the drug transaction, proceeds of crime, or otherwise tainted by criminality," Bodurtha said, adding that its potential use in the deal was "hypothetical."

The judge did rule that about $3,600 (C$5,000) in cash found in Sandeson's apartment after the murder was "offence-related property," meaning it will not be returned.

Sandeson has said the Bitcoin was worth between about $5,800 and $7,200 (C$8,000 to C$10,000), according to Global News. A lawyer representing Samson's family in a separate wrongful death lawsuit, in which the cryptocurrency had been at the center, has said it could now be worth more than $144,000 (C$200,000). Global News did not report how much Bitcoin the wallet holds.

Sandeson, then 23 and about to start medical school at Dalhousie University, arranged for Samson, 22, to come to his apartment on August 15, 2015, to sell him cannabis that Sandeson had arranged to buy for C$40,000, according to prosecutors at his 2023 trial. Sandeson shot Samson, kept the drugs and the money, and later admitted to dumping his body in a river that feeds the Bay of Fundy. Samson's remains have never been found.

Sandeson was convicted of first-degree murder in 2017, but an appeals court overturned the verdict in 2020. At a second trial in 2023, he admitted to shooting Samson but said he acted in self-defense. A jury found him guilty of second-degree murder, which carries an automatic life sentence. He is serving his sentence in Quebec and will be eligible for parole in 2030.

Understanding How Decentralized Finance Protocols Work

DeFi, or decentralized finance, works through smart contracts that coordinate financial activity on-chain. Instead of relying on a centralized intermediary, DeFi protocols use liquidity pools, automated market makers, collateral rules, oracles, governance systems, and composable protocol integrations to support trading, lending, yield strategies, derivatives, and other financial functions.

DeFi 201 is intended for readers who already understand crypto basics and want to understand how DeFi protocols actually work. It moves beyond beginner definitions and into the systems that keep decentralized finance running: exchanges, lending markets, yield strategies, oracle networks, derivatives, governance, and composability.

DeFi is best understood as a connected protocol system rather than a list of isolated apps. Its main components include decentralized exchanges, lending protocols, yield aggregators, oracles, decentralized derivatives, governance, and composability.

how decentralized exchanges enable on-chain trading through order books, AMMs, liquidity pools, and intent-based execution;

how DeFi lending markets use collateral, pooled liquidity, utilization, interest rates, and liquidations;

how yield aggregators use vaults, strategy routing, managers, and keepers to automate DeFi strategies;

why oracles are critical for prices, collateral values, liquidations, derivatives, and synthetic assets;

how decentralized derivatives create synthetic exposure through collateral, margin, funding, and liquidation mechanics;

how DAOs and governance tokens coordinate proposals, voting, delegation, treasuries, and protocol upgrades;

how composability lets protocols build on each other while creating dependency and systemic-risk trade-offs.

Explain how DEX architectures route trades and allocate liquidity.

Describe the mechanics and risks of DeFi lending protocols.

Explain the role of vaults and automated yield strategies.

Identify oracle dependencies and manipulation risk.

Describe how DeFi protocols package derivative exposure without centralized intermediaries.

Explain how DAOs coordinate protocol upgrades and incentives.

Analyze both the benefits and risks of DeFi composability.

The lesson summaries below are a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive DeFi 201 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities.

Compares on-chain order books, constant-product, concentrated-liquidity, constant-sum, and hybrid AMMs with intent-based routing by competing solvers.

Follows collateralized borrowing through pooled liquidity, utilization-based rates, supply and borrow APY, health factors, and liquidation mechanics.

Shows how vaults route deposits across strategies and automate compounding while adding smart-contract, strategy, fee, governance, and automation risk.

Explains how smart contracts obtain price and other external data and why source quality, aggregation, latency, manipulation resistance, and failure modes matter across DeFi.

Introduces perpetuals, options, and synthetic assets and connects their design to collateral, margin, funding, liquidation, oracle, and leverage risks.

Covers governance tokens, proposals, delegation, quorum, voting power, treasuries, protocol upgrades, and the risks of low participation or concentrated control.

Explains how protocols combine as money legos to create new products while dependencies can transmit smart-contract, oracle, collateral, bridge, or governance failures across DeFi.

DeFi means decentralized finance. It refers to financial protocols that run through blockchains and smart contracts rather than traditional intermediaries. In DeFi, users can trade, lend, borrow, supply liquidity, manage collateral, vote on protocol changes, or build products by connecting multiple protocols together.

The important idea is not that DeFi removes every kind of intermediation. It changes where coordination happens. Rules that would usually be enforced by a platform, broker, exchange, or bank can be encoded into smart contracts, governance systems, oracle feeds, and liquidity mechanisms.

Most DeFi protocols combine a few common building blocks: users, smart contracts, liquidity providers, traders, borrowers, lenders, governance participants, and external data providers. The exact mix depends on the protocol type.

Smart contracts: Encode the rules for trading, lending, collateral, fees, voting, or settlement.

Liquidity pools: Hold assets that traders or borrowers interact with.

Liquidity providers: Supply assets to pools and take protocol-specific risks.

Oracles: Bring external data, such as prices, into smart contracts.

Governance: Coordinates upgrades, parameters, incentives, and treasury decisions.

Composability: Lets protocols plug into each other and create new products.

Decentralized exchanges allow users to trade on-chain through smart contracts. Early exchange design borrowed from order books, where buyers and sellers post bids and asks. But on-chain order books can be expensive and capital-inefficient because each order update consumes gas and liquidity may sit idle.

Automated market makers changed that model. In an AMM, traders do not need to match with another person’s order. They trade against a shared liquidity pool supplied by liquidity providers. A liquidity pool is a smart contract that holds tokens, and an algorithmic formula determines prices based on the pool’s reserves.

The constant product AMM model uses the formula x times y equals k. It keeps the product of the two token reserves constant, so prices move automatically as traders buy one asset and add another. This model is simple and resilient, but it spreads liquidity across all possible prices, which can make capital inefficient.

Core idea: Matches bids and asks directly.

Trade-off: Costly and capital-inefficient on-chain.

Strength: Simple, always provides liquidity.

Trade-off: Capital may sit unused far from market price.

Strength: Higher capital efficiency and tighter spreads.

Trade-off: Requires more active liquidity management.

Core idea: Keeps exchange rate near fixed parity.

Trade-off: Can break if one side of the pool is drained.

Core idea: Blends product and sum curves.

Strength: Useful for stable or pegged assets.

Trade-off: More complex and less intuitive.

Core idea: Users express desired outcomes; solvers compete to fulfill them.

Strength: Can improve routing and user experience.

Trade-off: Depends on solver competition and execution quality.

Liquidity providers deposit assets into pools so other users can trade. In return, LPs may earn a share of trading fees. But providing liquidity is not passive income without risk. LP returns depend on trading volume, fee tiers, price movement, pool design, and impermanent loss.

LP profitability can be expressed as trading fees earned minus impermanent loss, if any.

DeFi lending protocols let users supply assets to earn yield and borrow against collateral without a traditional bank. Smart contracts replace bilateral lending relationships with pooled markets that set rules, manage collateral, and enforce liquidations automatically.

A typical lending protocol uses overcollateralization. A borrower deposits collateral, borrows a smaller value against it, and must keep the position healthy. If collateral value falls too far, the protocol can liquidate the position to protect the lending pool.

Collateral: Assets pledged to secure a loan or leveraged position.

Utilization: How much of a lending pool is currently borrowed.

Supply APY: The rate suppliers may earn for lending assets.

Borrow APY: The rate borrowers pay to use borrowed assets.

Health factor: A measure of whether a position is safely collateralized.

Liquidation: Forced sale or closure when a position becomes unsafe.

Yield aggregators simplify DeFi yield generation by routing deposits across strategies and automating parts of the process. Instead of manually moving funds between pools or protocols, users deposit into a vault. The aggregator then follows a strategy, compounds returns, and abstracts away some of the operational work.

This does not remove risk. Aggregators add another layer of smart-contract exposure, strategy risk, fee policy, governance risk, and dependence on keepers or automation agents. Yield optimization is a mechanism to understand, not a recommendation.

DeFi protocols often need information that does not naturally live on-chain. Lending markets need asset prices to value collateral. Derivatives need reference prices. Synthetic assets need external data. Liquidations depend on timely and accurate price information.

Oracles provide this data to smart contracts. Because smart contracts can execute automatically based on oracle inputs, oracle design is a core security issue. Bad data, delayed data, manipulation, or concentrated data sources can create losses across trading, lending, derivatives, and liquidation systems.

More resilient designs combine multiple sources and aggregate observations before publishing a value on-chain. That can reduce dependence on one provider, but it does not eliminate latency, source correlation, or governance risk.

Decentralized derivatives create exposure to assets or market outcomes without necessarily requiring users to hold the underlying asset directly. Common examples include perpetual futures, options, synthetic assets, and other collateralized instruments.

The key mechanics include collateral, margin, funding rates, liquidation thresholds, and protocol risk controls. Perpetual futures have no expiry and use funding payments to help keep contract prices aligned with spot prices. Like other DeFi products, derivatives can increase capital efficiency but also introduce leverage, liquidation, oracle, and systemic-risk concerns.

Many DeFi protocols are governed through DAOs, governance tokens, proposals, voting systems, delegation, and treasuries. Governance determines how protocols update parameters, allocate incentives, manage upgrades, and respond to risk.

Proposals may need a quorum or other participation threshold before a vote can take effect. The exact rules determine how voting power is counted, how delegates act, and how quickly a protocol can respond to changing conditions.

Governance can make protocols more community-driven, but it can also create concentration and coordination problems. Token-weighted voting may give large holders outsized influence. Low voter participation can make decisions fragile. Delegation can improve expertise but may also centralize practical control.

Composability is the ability for DeFi protocols to plug into and build on top of one another. This is why DeFi is often described as money legos. A lending protocol can use an oracle, a yield aggregator can route deposits across lending markets, and a derivatives protocol can depend on multiple liquidity and data systems.

Composability accelerates innovation because developers can reuse existing liquidity, infrastructure, and protocol primitives. But it also creates dependency risk. If one widely used protocol, oracle, bridge, collateral asset, or governance decision fails, the effects can cascade across many connected applications.

What it does: Enables on-chain trading through pools, curves, routing, or intents.

Main risk: Slippage, LP risk, smart-contract risk, solver/routing risk.

What it does: Lets users supply assets and borrow against collateral.

Main risk: Liquidation, collateral volatility, oracle risk.

What it does: Automates deposits, routing, strategies, and compounding.

Main risk: Strategy risk, contract risk, fee/governance risk.

What it does: Supplies external data to smart contracts.

Main risk: Data manipulation, latency, source concentration.

What it does: Creates synthetic or leveraged exposure.

Main risk: Funding, liquidation, margin, oracle, and leverage risk.

What it does: Coordinates protocol decisions and upgrades.

Main risk: Voter concentration, low participation, governance capture.

What it does: Connects multiple protocols into new products.

Main risk: Dependency and cascading failure risk.

DeFi replaces some intermediaries with code, liquidity systems, and governance. That does not remove risk. It changes the form of risk.

Smart contract risk: code can contain bugs or be exploited.

Oracle risk: bad or delayed data can trigger wrong pricing, lending, or liquidation outcomes.

Liquidity risk: pools can become shallow, imbalanced, or expensive to trade against.

Liquidation risk: collateralized positions can be closed when markets move quickly.

Governance risk: token voting can be captured, delayed, or dominated by large holders.

Composability risk: protocols that depend on one another can transmit failures across the system.

Regulatory risk: DeFi protocols, interfaces, and participants may face changing legal treatment.

This page is for educational purposes and explains protocol mechanics. It does not provide investment, trading, tax, or legal advice.

A user wants to trade ETH for USDC through a decentralized exchange. Instead of matching with a specific seller, the user trades against an ETH/USDC liquidity pool. Liquidity providers have deposited both assets into the pool. The smart contract calculates the trade based on the pool’s pricing formula, updates the token reserves, charges a trading fee, and sends the output token to the user.

The user gets an on-chain swap. LPs earn fees. The pool’s price changes because its reserves changed. If the trade is large relative to pool liquidity, the user may experience slippage. If the pool is part of a larger aggregator or intent-based route, solvers or routers may search across multiple liquidity sources to improve execution.

DeFi protocols use smart contracts to coordinate financial activity without a traditional centralized intermediary.

DEXs and AMMs use liquidity pools and algorithmic pricing to support on-chain trading.

DeFi lending protocols use collateral, utilization, rates, and liquidations to manage risk.

Yield aggregators automate strategy routing and compounding, but they add another layer of protocol risk.

Oracles are critical because many DeFi systems depend on accurate external data.

Decentralized derivatives introduce collateral, margin, funding, leverage, and liquidation dynamics.

Governance and composability are major strengths of DeFi, but they also create coordination and systemic-risk trade-offs.

This is an intermediate topic. Helpful background knowledge includes blockchain basics, Ethereum basics, wallets, tokens, smart contracts, basic trading terms, and basic lending vocabulary.

Related Campus topics include Ethereum & Layer 1s 201 for smart contracts, gas, and token standards; Market Structure 201 for liquidity, order books, derivatives, and institutions; Scaling & Layer 2s 201 for cheaper execution environments and rollup context; and stablecoins, RWAs, and glossary pages for collateral, settlement, and liquidity context.

DEX: A decentralized exchange that lets users trade through smart contracts rather than a centralized intermediary.

AMM: An automated market maker that prices trades algorithmically using pooled liquidity.

Liquidity pool: A smart contract holding tokens supplied by liquidity providers for traders to swap against.

Liquidity provider: A user or entity that deposits assets into a pool and earns fees while taking pool risk.

Constant product AMM: An AMM model that preserves the invariant x times y equals k.

Concentrated liquidity: A liquidity design that lets LPs provide capital inside selected price ranges.

Intent-based DEX: A DEX model where users express desired outcomes and solvers compete to execute them.

Collateral: Assets pledged to secure a DeFi loan or leveraged position.

Liquidation: The forced closing or sale of collateral when a position becomes unsafe.

Yield aggregator: A protocol that routes funds across strategies to optimize yield.

Oracle: A service that provides external data, such as prices, to smart contracts.

Perpetual futures: Derivative contracts with no expiry that use funding rates to track spot prices.

DAO: A decentralized organization governed through proposals, votes, and smart-contract rules.

Governance token: A token used to vote on protocol decisions or delegate voting power.

Composability: The ability for protocols to plug into and build on top of one another.

DeFi lending protocols let users supply assets to earn yield or borrow against collateral through smart-contract-based lending markets.

#5057. What Olympic Gold Medalist Tara Davis-Woodhall Uses to Recover After Her Hardest Training Days

The workout gear and personal must-haves that help her feel ready anywhere.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Winner of a gold medal at the 2024 Summer Olympics. Winner of the silver medal in the 2023 World Championships. Coach at Kansas State University. These are just a few ways to describe the track and field phenom Tara Davis-Woodhall.

Women’s Health recently got the chance to pick Davis-Woodhall’s brain about her fitness gear essentials—the training and recovery tools she can’t live without. Consider this her list of training must-haves. And some of her picks might surprise you (hint: one of them smells really good).

These slides with built-in heat and vibration have become Davis-Woodhall’s favorite way to recover after training (our feet need recovery, too!) “The heat and vibration feel incredible after long days, and they’re so comfortable that I honestly don't want to take them off,” Davis-Woodhall tells Women’s Health.

She slips them on after practice, when she’s traveling, and whenever it feels like her feet need a little extra TLC. One of the reasons these slides have become her go-to is that since they’re footwear, she can still multitask while her feet are getting the recovery benefits of heat and vibration therapy. “I love that I can recover while still moving around and winding down after a long day,” she says.

While journaling may not be the first thing that pops into your mind when you think “fitness essentials of a pro athlete,” Davis-Woodhall considers it an essential training tool. “My journal is always with me because it’s where I can slow down, reset, and get my thoughts out of my head,” she tells WH. “I use it to write down goals, reflect on training and competitions, and keep track of the little things that are working for me.”

Training isn’t the only thing Davis-Woodhall examines and processes during her journaling, which she says has become a really important part of her routine. “Sometimes it’s about track & field, but sometimes I also just need a moment to write and reset, “ she says.

Hydration is important for all of us, but even more so for athletes performing at the highest level. “Hydration is a huge part of my routine,” Davis-Woodhall says. She has additional dehydrating demands on her body outside of training like extensive traveling and spending a lot of time training outdoors.

While there are many electrolyte supplements on the market, Davis-Woodhall has found her favorite in Cadence. It helps her stay consistent because she enjoys the taste, especially the Melonberry and Orange Soda flavors. “I drink it before, during, and after training to help replace the electrolytes I'm losing and stay hydrated. I also love that it has zero sugar and no caffeine, so I can drink it throughout the day.”

Last year, a study examining the effects of athletes using music to boost mood, and that that mood boost can in turn have a positive impact on physical performance. Davis-Woodhall is no stranger to using music as a tool in her training. “I never go anywhere without my headphones,” she says. “Whether I’m warming up, cooling down, traveling, or just need a little time in my own world, music is such a big part of how I get into the right mindset.”

But getting hyped and ready isn’t the only time Davis-Woodhall taps into music to help her maintain peak performance. Sometimes she uses her headphones to tune out distractions and reset.

We love the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Bluetooth Headphones, our pick for best noise cancelling headphones, for doing just that.

Music isn’t the only thing that can get you in the right frame of mind. A signature scent can, too. “I love a good fragrance, and BOSS Bottled Beyond is one I always have with me,” Davis-Woodhall says. “I love the scent, but I also love what it represents: feeling confident, powerful, and lifting up the women around you.”

Davis-Woodhall wears this fragrance when she’s getting ready for competition but also reaches for it in her day-to-day life. “It's one of those little things that makes me feel put together and ready for whatever I'm walking into,” she says.

To help keep her legs fresh and ready, Davis-Woodhall knows that supporting healthy leg circulation is crucial. A device she uses to help with this is Firefly, a wireless band that wraps around the top of the calf and emits stimulating pulses that mimic the muscle contractions of walking, which helps increase circulation. “Between training, competing, and constantly traveling, recovery is such a huge part of what I do. I love Firefly because it’s small enough to keep in my track bag, so I can use it right after training,” she says, noting that it’s become a tool she relies on all season.

The best recovery tools that we use in our routines are sometimes the simplest. Case in point: the yoga mat and massage ball Davis-Woodhall keeps on hand. “I always have these around for stretching, mobility, and working through any tight spots after training or in the middle of a competition. I use the roller ball a lot on my feet and legs, and the yoga mat gives me a place to go through my normal stretching and mobility routine.”

The Manuka Pro yoga mat is one that WH editors love for its extra thickness and no-slip surface, and the Rad Rounds set of three different sizes of massage balls with different densities will cover any spot you’re trying to release.

WH editors love compression boots, and so does Davis-Woodhall, particularly the Hyperice Normatec Elite Legs. “This is my go-to after my hardest training days, especially after long sprint days since I started hurdling again this season,” she says. “My legs can definitely feel heavy after those workouts, so I usually put them on in the evening while Hunter and I are relaxing or watching TV.” While Davis-Woodhall uses these compression boots throughout her season, she is especially consistent leading into a competition to make sure her legs feel fresh and ready to jump.

Natascha is an editor and writer covering health, fitness, and the ways people move through the world. #5056. Bitcoin bounces from 7-week low under $76K as Democrats sweep Congress

Bitcoin price downside reached a seven-week-low of $75,618 as 24-hour crypto long liquidations neared $300 million.

Bitcoin (BTC) sought to erase 3% overnight losses on Wednesday as crypto markets digested the Democratic sweep of the midterm elections.

Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD falling into Tuesday’s daily close as election results came in, with Democrats going on to win control of both the House and Senate. The pair dropped to a low of $75,618 on Bitstamp, a level last seen on Sept. 16, before rebounding as high as $78,039 over the next three hours.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Data from CoinGlass showed the price dip liquidating late BTC long positions below $76,000, while a wall of asks kept upside contained below $78,000. Total crypto long liquidations over the past 24 hours stood at $288 million.

BTC liquidation heatmap. Source: CoinGlass

In comments sent to Cointelegraph, Kelly Ye, head of research at institutional digital asset trading platform Talos, said that markets had largely priced in the election outcome.

“Bitcoin moved about 1.7% after the polls closed, close to the roughly 1.8% options had priced, and there was no major leverage flush. The election was the main event, but markets had largely prepared for it,” she said.

US stock futures showed similar moves, initially falling before recouping some losses. S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures were both down by about 0.3% at the time of writing.

S&P 500 futures one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Late Tuesday, Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at financial services company Ameriprise Financial, told CNBC that concerns over data-center and broader AI capital expenditure were producing an adverse market reaction to the Democratic gains.

“If you get some governorships that are Democratic, what does that mean for the data center buildout, which has already seen a lot of skepticism over the last couple weeks in terms of the hyperscaler capex spending?” he asked.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, US President Donald Trump, who previously said he could become “Mr. Veto” to block Democratic policy initiatives, struck a conciliatory tone.

“I think we’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll get along very well with them,” he said.

Bitcoin’s drop to $75,618 coincided with its 50-week simple moving average (SMA), a trend line that has held as support since mid-September.

Related: Here’s what happened in crypto today

In an analysis posted on X, Keith Alan, co-founder of crypto trading suite Material Indicators, identified the 50-week SMA as a line in the sand for Bitcoin bulls. Failure to defend it, he argued, would open the door to a “deeper correction ahead.”

BTC/USD one-day chart with 50 SMA. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Crypto trader and analyst Rekt Capital, who had forecast BTC/USD dipping below $76,000 after a failed breakout attempt above $78,000, continued to flag overhead resistance on the three-day chart.

“If this continues then these newfound 3-Day Lower Highs may guide price back towards the ~$75.5k level below over time,” he said on Wednesday.

BTC/USD three-day chart. Source: Rekt Capital on X.com

#5055. BitGo launches institutional trading and financial solutions business led by former NYDIG executive

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Pete Janney will lead the new BitGo Global Markets division, following the firm's acquisition of NYDIG’s institutional and trading business in August.

Digital asset infrastructure firm BitGo Holdings BitGo Holdings, Inc. (BTGO) announced the launch of BitGo Global Markets on Wednesday, its new institutional trading and financial solutions business bringing together global liquidity, execution, financing, derivatives, and settlement services.

The division will be headed up by former NYDIG executive Pete Janney following BitGo's acquisition of NYDIG's institutional and trading business on Aug. 27, according to a statement shared exclusively with The Block.

About 30 employees joined BitGo following the NYDIG acquisition, bringing experience in derivatives, financing, collateral servicing, and structured products. Janney initially came aboard as head of financial infrastructure and brings extensive experience in trading and capital markets.

BitGo has been offering institutional trading through BitGo Prime since 2020, with that business becoming part of Global Markets alongside the expanded derivatives, collateral management, and structured finance solutions from NYDIG.

"BitGo has built a strong foundation across custody, liquidity, trading, financing, and settlement," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe said in the statement. "Global Markets brings these capabilities together with deeper capital markets expertise, allowing us to support more complex institutional strategies and serve a broader range of our clients' financial needs. Pete understands how institutions trade and manage risk, and I'm excited to have him leading Global Markets.”

Under the new unit, BitGo's Global Liquidity Layer will provide access to spot trading and large over-the-counter transactions, drawing liquidity from exchanges, market makers, and other counterparties, the firm said. Clients can also borrow against their crypto holdings to fund trading positions, with BitGo keeping the collateral in qualified custody, monitoring margins, and handling collateral calls or liquidations when needed.

Additionally, BitGo Global Markets will offer options, swaps, and custom structured products for eligible counterparties to hedge exposure, express market views, and manage portfolio risk, the firm said.

Global Markets will also provide managed investment strategies, private funds, and research, while BitGo's Go Network will handle clearing and settlement.

"Clients who own digital assets need sophisticated solutions that go beyond buy and hold," Janney said. "I look forward to accelerating that work and growing the Global Markets franchise at BitGo."

BTGO was trading up 3.4% in pre-market trading on Wednesday, according to TradingView, following a 3.7% rise on Tuesday.

#5054. I Got a Six-Pack in 28 Days. Here’s the Plan I Used.

Thanks to the 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout and key lifestyle changes, my abs are defined and strong.

I HAVE ALWAYS envied the chiseled bodies of the models, bodybuilders, and celebrities I’ve profiled as a fitness writer. But looking like a beautiful statue-person is a 24/7 chore, and pizza tastes damn good. Then, sometime after learning my wife was pregnant, and amid my attempt to bring order to every crevice of my life, I was offered a chance to try a new training program from Men's Health: 28-Day Belly Fat Burner. I followed the plan for four weeks and ultimately shed 13 pounds and lost three inches from my waist. It was packed with science-backed tips for getting lean, plus a 28-day workout plan. You can get started today by accessing the 28-day plan via your MVP membership here or if you want the full guided experience you can get the book here.

The 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout, created by Men’s Health Advisory Board member David Otey, CSCS, breaks down like this:

Since I started lifting weights in 2012, my body weight has fluctuated aggressively every few years. Like most guys, I’d white-knuckle my way through a diet only to regain the pounds shortly thereafter. And then, in the fall of 2022, weighing 210 pounds and in the middle of another training lull, I committed to making lifestyle changes. I walked more, drank less alcohol, counted calories, began lifting weights consistently again, and didn’t let a cheat meal become a cheat week. It wasn’t easy, and there were (many) slip-ups, but consistency prevailed, and I lost 25 pounds in about seven months.

Not too long after, I began to ease up on my diet and training, and my weight plateaued at 185 pounds—considerably lighter than I was once, but still far from ripped.

With this transformation in the rearview mirror, it’s easier for me to conduct a post-mortem on my old lifting routine and pinpoint how the 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout patched up some now-obvious holes in it. Here’s what I loved about this program:

Before, I was only training three times a week, doing a few sets for my legs, zero direct core work, and around six sets for every major muscle except my back. While I was maybe maintaining muscle, my old routine wasn’t pushing my gains forward like the 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout did.

Research within the last five years suggests you need at least 10 sets per muscle per week to stimulate muscle growth, and a 2022 meta-analysis, co-authored by Men’s Health contributor and exercise scientist Brad Schoenfeld, PhD, CSCS, found that same number of sets helped spare lean muscle tissue in subjects eating a calorie-restricted diet.

This program certainly provides enough sets per muscle. While direct total volume for certain muscle groups, mainly the biceps and triceps, fell under that 10-set recommendation, implementing compound exercises, which usually target more than one muscle, provides enough stimulus to those smaller, ancillary muscle groups. (E.g., barbell rows and pullups mainly work your back, but your biceps get some play, too.)

And even though this routine is designed for those losing weight, Otey factors progressive overload into the program. Each week, I performed either more reps or lifted heavier weights, which helped me preserve my strength and muscle. I didn’t make significant strength gains—for example, I bench-pressed 60-pound dumbbells for three sets of eight reps during week two and then for 10 reps two weeks later—but the incremental progression meant my gains were moving in the right direction.

I didn’t take a body fat test, so I can’t say with certainty that zero ounces of muscle was lost. Still, my arms only shrunk a quarter of an inch while I lost three inches from my waist.

My heart rate was usually between 140 and 170 beats per minute (BPM) during each 28-Day Belly Fat Burner workout. Sustaining that pace for 20 to 30 minutes while lifting weights was new to me, and as a result, I burned roughly 20 to 30 percent more calories per minute during these workouts than in my previous workouts, according to my Apple Watch. I also performed the same number of exercises as in my old workouts (five to six per session) in less than half the time.

The short, full-body workouts ensured I never felt too fatigued and never left my muscles overly sore. I’m unsure how I would have fared during this 28-day program otherwise. In those regards, the program seemed specifically tailored for someone in a fat loss phase.

Not only was intensity lacking in my previous program, but I was doing the same exercises for the same reps each week. While research on the effects of exercise variation is sparse, current evidence suggests that systematically switching through exercises that hit the target muscle and are joint-friendly can have a positive impact on muscle gain in your training. (Conversely, switching it up too often can negatively affect your gains.) The main takeaway: You should have a short list of exercises you love for each muscle and cycle through them every few weeks.

The alternating weekly workouts in Men’s Health’s plan also provided me a mental reprieve from the handful of monotonous lifestyle changes I made to get leaner while on this program. I walked the same route twice a day, ate the same meal three times a day, and popped a melatonin gummy every night at 10. The motivation I felt from following the 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout carried over to the rest of my routine, which made it easy to not just stick to the plan but crush it with enthusiasm.

People train for progress, and when that progress stalls like mine did, it’s difficult to get excited about your routine. In my old workouts, I was going through the motions, performing easy exercises with modest intensity. Most of the time, I didn’t even break a sweat. If my goal were to walk 10,000 steps daily, I’d usually fall short at 7,000. My desire to get back on my macros after an unplanned meal waned. More and more, I was eating out and snacking. The physical changes I saw while doing Belly Fat Burner motivated me to keep going and give it my all.

LOSING FAT REQUIRES much more than just lifting weights, so I had to work on implementing other habits while following the 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout. I ate more protein (one gram per pound of body weight) to help me stay full and maintain my muscle mass while in a caloric deficit. I walked between 15,000 and 20,000 steps daily to increase my NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis), I didn’t stop training in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu or kickboxing because I like those sports, and more activity equals more calories burned. Lastly, I made sure to get seven hours of sleep, nightly. To improve my sleep efficiency, I kept my phone out of my bedroom and cut out alcohol completely (which also hinders fat loss and is high in empty calories).

Those habits helped me get as lean as possible while I followed the 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout. If this sounds overwhelming, well, it was a lot to manage, but the program made sticking with it all easier. The brief, high-intensity workouts burned a lot of calories in a short amount of time and kept me feeling fresh session to session. Also, the challenge of tackling new exercises in a new format provided me with enough motivation to grind through the other aspects of my plan. It was tough but fun.

I’m proud of myself for sticking to a routine that I would never have even considered attempting just six months ago. The 28-Day Belly Fat Burner Workout is a time-efficient, simple, and efficacious program. It forced me to push myself harder in the gym and helped me maintain muscle as I choked down 96 percent lean beef and green beans for a month.

Now that I have a rock-hard midsection…all that’s really changed is now I need new clothes. Achieving the look I’ve wanted for a decade or so feels great, though. Better yet, following this program was a much-needed change that reinvigorated my motivation to train hard, try new exercises, and recalibrate my lifestyle.

#5053. Midterms Blue Wave Makes $917K for One Polymarket Trader, If Alaska Doesn’t Flip

Midterms Blue Wave Makes $917K for One Polymarket Trader, If Alaska Doesn’t Flip

A "blue wave” swept the U.S. midterms as the Democrats took control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, in a crushing blow to President Donald Trump.

Polymarket predictor 0xA2 is the platform's most profitable trader over the past 24 hours, according to the site's daily leaderboard. They are currently $917,000 in profit, although most of that is still in an active position that has a real (ableit small) chance of upset.

The user wagered $609,644 on the Republicans not winning any Senate swing states when odds sat at just 36%, a market which has since surged to 87%. This turned his stake in to $1.48 million, putting him $860,000 in the green.

Its important to remember: these are unrealized gains and could drop at any moment as 0xA2 waits for Alaska's final verdict. Polymarket traders put a 14% chance on an upset—and while this may seem small, the site has seen similarly sized upsets recently—as in the case of Brazil's presidential election two weeks ago.

0xA2 also profited $106,115 by predicting that the Democrats would win the Texas Senate—profits that have been realized. Oddly, the user's second largest active position is $1.42 million on the U.S. not confirming that aliens exist before 2027.

"Election night showed how quickly round-the-clock markets move when traditional exchanges are closed. As polls began closing at 6pm ET, Kalshi’s odds of a Democratic sweep went from about 74% to 99%," Kelly Ye, Head of Research at digital asset management firm Talos, said in a note shared with Decrypt. "Prediction-market trading peaked between 8pm and 10pm ET, led by a small number of large trades."

It was a big day for Polymarket users profiting, with the top 10 users on the platform profiting more than $170,000, per the leaderboard. To put that into perspective, on a fairly random day in March this year, the top daily winner on Polymarket profited $154,000, according to the WayBackMachine, and the 10th biggest winner that day gained $29,700.

The midterms attracted major activity on leading prediction markets Polymarket and Kalshi. According to Precition.com data, midterm markets attracted more than $546 million in notional volume over the past two weeks.

"The 2024 election was the breakthrough moment for prediction markets. It was their first major real-world test and the event that really drove volume and open interest," Dash, the pseudonymous data lead at Prediction.com, told Decrypt. "Today, sports dominate trading volume, but Politics is still the key driving factor for open interest."

During the 2024 presidential race, Polymarket became what Bernstein analysts called the world’s largest election prediction market, with its flagship market topping $3.6 billion in volume. Maybe more importantly, predictors favored Trump for most of the campaign, while traditional polls kept him neck and neck with Kamala Harris. Prediction market users took this as a sign that prediction markets are more accurate than traditional political polling.

"Increasingly, people are looking for accurate forecasts on election results," Dash said, "and prediction markets are one place they can be found."

Those forecasts aren't always accurate, though. Just two weeks ago, Polymarket predictors whiffed Brazil's presidential election, with users giving Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva about a 20% chance of winning ahead of election day, before he ultimately beat Flávio Bolsonaro to take a fourth term.

Experts told Decrypt at the time that Brazil’s prediction market ban had left the odds in the hands of traders with little local knowledge to correct the odds. Plus, experts warned that a 20% chance of something happening is still a very real chance.

"Ultimately, something that has an 80% chance of happening does not happen 20% of the time," Luke Nolan, senior researcher at CoinShares, said.

So that 14% chance that 0xA2 loses his $860,000 in profit should be taken seriously.

#5052. The 6 Best Dermaplaning Tools to Use at Home, Tested by Editors and Dermatologists

Dermaflash's Luxe Plus Device came out on top in our testing.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Dermaplaning is the biggest game changer in my beauty routine, which is saying a lot as a beauty editor who has tried every facial hair removal method. It's an exfoliating procedure that uses a blade to scrape the skin's surface to remove dead skin cells, dirt, debris, and peach fuzz, says dermatologist Azadeh Shirazi, MD. "When your skin is hairless and buildup-free, it looks super toned and bright." Plus, a freshly shaved face allows my serums and moisturizers to absorb deeper, and my makeup to glide on easier. Dermaplaning is my tool of choice for facial hair removal.

And here's the thing: You could splurge on a pricey salon service with a trained aesthetician, but I'm all about the DIY approach. While a professional treatment is more precise, at-home dermaplaning is cheaper, faster, and more convenient, especially since I have a busy schedule.

My guide is a good place to start your shopping, but you might want to also keep these pointers in mind if you're in the market for a new dermaplaning tool—or you're finally ready to try one for the first time.

Dr. Shirazi says the most important factor to consider is a blade that is made from a durable, high-quality material. The best devices I've tested feature a stainless steel blade. That's because Dr. Shirazi says it's easy to clean, is resistant to rust, and is super sharp.

When dermaplaning I prefer devices with a grippy handle, which helps control my strokes for a precise shave. More specifically, look for a tool that has a weighted handle, Dr. Shirazi says. "It should be long and have a good grip as you make the strokes on the skin." Some devices have rubber grippers for extra grip.

At-home skincare tools have become increasingly popular, and there are so many options to choose from, so I took matters into my own hands to carefully research the most popular and top-rated dermaplaning tools. After narrowing my choices to 12 picks, I tested these contenders before finalizing my list. I examined the safety features, blade materials, effectiveness, and comfort to ensure these are truly the best dermaplaning tools in the game. I spent several months testing these devices to ensure they're totally worth your hard-earned money.

And to ensure that there were a slew of options across all budgets, I tapped WH contributor Lily Wohlner, two dermatologists, and an aesthetician for their guidance. Ultimately, we only liked these six dermaplaning tools. We think you'll like them too.

Dermaflash earned major snaps from me, Wohlner, and Dr. Camp, so I knew it was our clear best overall pick. This high-tech gadget has a gentle pulsing technology and a super sharp blade to remove peach fuzz and dead skin cells in one fell swoop.

It provides an in-spa experience from the comfort of my bathroom. I'm always *shook* at how super smooth my face looks and feels after using the Dermaflash. The combo of tiny corrugations along the blade and gentle pulsing technology removes peach fuzz and dead skin cells swiftly without any nicks. The entire treatment is just a few minutes, making it a wonderful treat for busy women like myself.

The exfoliation leaves my skin more luminous before applying face moisturizer. Plus, my liquid, cream, and powder makeup applies easily, and caking is non-existent since using this device. My serums and moisturizer also sink in so quickly. I see the best results when I use it every two weeks, but honestly, I use it closer to every month, and it feels like such a treat.

Yes, this is by far the most expensive option on the list, but it's worth the splurge because it provides such a close shave in seconds. The Dermaflash feels so sturdy and comfortable to use in my hand that even relative dermaplaning beginners like myself can feel confident removing peach fuzz. The sharp blade ensures I get a close shave without scratching my sensitive skin, and the thick handle makes it easier to control.

The stainless blades are not as sharp as some of the other options on this list—and that’s OK. They do a solid job of removing dead skin cells and peach fuzz, but I’ll need to use Kitsch more frequently to achieve similar results as pricier alternatives, like Stackedskincare. But for the affordable price, they get the job done for an at-home tool.

Unlike the Dermaflash Luxe or the Versed Dermaplaning Tool, these disposable blades are packaged in sets of 12, so it's a one-and-done situation. You have enough tools to use one monthly and it'll last you for an entire year which is pretty sweet.

If you don't want to carry a big electric device on long vacations or need a handy option on the go, these will be your buddies. With my busy schedule, I always throw these into my bag when I'm short on time to dermaplane before a weekend trip.

I keep a few stashed in my cosmetic bag in case of a beauty emergency. These disposable powerhouses are the perfect addition to my routine when I'm traveling because they're lightweight and I can throw them away when I'm done dermaplaning my face and will never have to worry about them again.

I've found that applying a gentle oil to my skin before using these blades works wonders. It creates a smooth glide that transforms a regular at-home dermaplaning session into a luxurious spa-like experience.

This device has two options: a precision blade for targeting tricky spots like the upper lip, and a larger blade for covering the forehead and cheeks. Each tool comes with a single large blade, and the precise model is purchased separately.

I love how easy it is to switch between the two blades. Just pop on the clear plastic safety cover over the blade, slide the current head off, then slide the replacement blade with its new lid on and you're good to go.

The compact precision head has a smooth blade that quickly grooms the brows, upper lip, and precise areas of the chin where little hairs might pop up.

Regardless of which blade I opt for, I found they both provide a super close shave. Stacked glides easily across my face and eased my fear of accidentally cutting myself. And Dr. Camp backs me up, saying Stacked can improve the skin's tone and texture with consistent use.

If you don't want to spend a lot of money on an electric dermaplaning tool, opt for this suuuper affordable one from Spa Sciences. It uses sonic technology and a disposable blade to instantly remove peach fuzz, buildup, and dead skin. Associate fashion and commerce editor Lily Wohlner found that one treatment lasts a month, so you get more bang for your buck.

It has 250-plus movements per second to smooth the skin in seconds. Wohlner likes that it comes in three vibration settings, and she used the lowest speed during my first few treatments to avoid nicks and scratches. While each treatment lasts a month, she likes to incorporate this device into her skincare routine once a week to keep her face consistently smooth and clear.

Versed is Dr. Shirazi's no-fail recommendation, and it's popular among WH readers. Sadly, Versed is discontinuing this beloved tool, but they still have some in stock that you can buy immediately. Need two more reasons to shop right now? They're discounted by $10 when you order directly from Versed. Only 12 are available on Amazon, so once they're gone, they're gone forever.

So what makes them so great? While it can be tricky to dermaplane yourself, Dr. Shirazi credits the weighted round handle with providing ample control during each sesh. Despite the relatively affordable cost, it's made with high-quality materials, including the single edge, stainless steel blades that give the closest exfoliation treatment possible, she says.

No wonder it's also a fan-favorite pick among Amazon reviewers. With a 4.1-star average from more than 110 reviewers, Versed earned major snaps for being gentle on sensitive skin without compromising on a close shave. This pick features a stainless steel blade that removes peach fuzz and dead skin cells just as well as pricier alternatives that cost four times as much.

Another perk? Each replacement blade lasts three or four uses, so you're really getting a bang for your buck with this one. Versed recommends using the device every one to three weeks but avoid combining it with other exfoliation methods like scrubs and peels. When you're done, top your skin off with a hydrating serum, like my new favorite iSClinical Hydra-Cool Serum.

Prefer something that’s tried and true with thousands of Amazon reviews? Look no further than Schick Touch-Up. It’s the kind of $5 Amazon find that’ll make you rethink blind buys.

For starters, Schick hits pretty much all of the key factors you want in a manual dermaplaning tool, such as a stainless steel blade and protective cap. But what thousands of Amazon shoppers appreciate most is that it works for both the brows and face. Plus, the vibrant shades also make the tool easy to spot in your makeup bag. No wonder Schick is the No. 1 best seller on Amazon. It’s affordable and effective, and it has amassed 152,600 perfect 5-star Amazon reviews.

Truly, the only downside is mastering your dermaplaning technique. Some reviewers accidentally nicked their face by applying too much pressure. To avoid this, pull your face taut, slowly glide the blade across the skin, and don’t shave over the same spot twice.

Doing treatments at home (versus in-office) and the results they bring are slightly trickier to predict and come with more risks, especially the chance of infections, scarring, or skin damage, cautions Dr. Shirazi. Her advice is to take it slow and try it only if you're comfortable. It's important to thoroughly cleanse the area you'll be treating, clean your hands, sanitize the tools, and tidy up the space, she says. "Be informed about dermaplaning—the more you know, the better you can assess the risks."

Keep in mind that dermaplaning might not suit those with sensitive or acne-prone skin. "You need a strong skin barrier to tolerate the treatment, so if you have dry skin or flaking red skin, it’s best to let the skin heal before dermaplaning," she says. "It can also worsen certain skin conditions like acne, psoriasis, eczema, and hives."

The number one no-no when it comes to dermaplaning: Don't over-exfoliate. "If you are on retinoids or exfoliants like glycolic or salicylic acid, you need to stop them a week before," says Dr. Shirazi. She also warns against dermaplaning if you have active wounds or skin conditions such as eczema and active wounds, as your skin needs to heal fully before dermaplaning. Lastly, don’t forget to thoroughly cleanse both the skin and hands before using the tool.

If you don't know how to use an at-home dermaplaning device, follow these simple steps with your manual or electric tool: Place the device at a 90-degree angle on the skin, starting at the top of the cheekbone near the hairline. Hold the skin taut as you gently glide the tool toward your nose. Continue until you have covered the entire cheek and jaw area. Repeat these steps across the forehead, lip, and chin.

Dermaplaning can be performed once every four to eight weeks, according to Dr. Shirazi. However, some brands recommend using their specific tools more often. Make sure to read the label on your device or consult your dermatologist if you're unsure how often to use your tool.

#5051. Circle reports $865 million in Q3 revenue and reserve income, discloses 5% workforce reduction

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Circle booked $182 million in ARC token presale revenue during the quarter, while income from its USDC reserves fell.

Stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group Circle Internet Group, Inc. (CRCL) reported $865 million in total revenue and reserve income for the third quarter, up 17% from a year earlier, according to its earnings release on Wednesday.

Net income from continuing operations came in at $226 million, compared with $214.4 million in the same quarter last year. Adjusted EBITDA was $317 million, up from $171.5 million in Q3 2025. Circle previously reported $701 million in revenue and reserve income for the second quarter of this year, naming BlackRock, DTCC, and Visa among founding validators for its Arc blockchain.

Operating expenses rose 16% year over year to $245 million in the third quarter, the firm said, citing higher administrative, IT infrastructure, and marketing costs. Distribution, transaction, and other costs fell 8% to $412 million, mostly due to lower distribution payments, it added.

A footnote to the earnings tables also disclosed that Circle had reduced its workforce by approximately 5%, with the company booking $9.1 million in associated restructuring expenses, mainly for notice period and severance payments, employee benefits, and related costs. Circle said the reduction was designed to "better align our organizational structure with our operating model and strategic priorities," but did not give a headcount for the cuts. Circle had approximately 1,100 employees worldwide at the end of 2025, according to its annual report.

Of the $207 million Circle reported in other revenue, $182 million was recognized in Q3 from its ARC token presale. Other revenue had totaled $29 million in the third quarter of 2025. Circle agreed to sell a total of $242.2 million worth of ARC tokens in the presale at a purchase price of $0.30 per token and a $3 billion fully diluted valuation. Circle attributed the 85% increase in adjusted EBITDA to the presale revenue and lower distribution costs, partly offset by spending on new products.

Circle also maintained its full-year 2026 guidance, including $310 million to $330 million in other revenue and $570 million to $585 million in adjusted operating expenses.

Reserve income fell 8% year over year to $658 million as its reserve return rate declined by 61 basis points, the firm said. Circle's USDC stablecoin averaged $73.3 billion in circulation during Q3, an 8% increase from a year earlier. Onchain USDC transaction volume reached $13.9 trillion for the quarter, up 49% year over year. USDC circulation stood at $73.9 billion at quarter-end, unchanged from a year earlier, while Circle's stablecoin market share fell to 27%.

Circle opened Arc's public mainnet on Sept. 16, with more than 100 institutional and ecosystem builders on the network at launch. It also minted the initial supply of 10 billion ARC tokens, which the firm said was a technical milestone, not a commitment to launch them publicly. It expects Arc to move from proof of authority to proof of stake in 2027.

In September, Circle also agreed to acquire Tazapay, a Singapore-based payments firm with more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume. The firm expects the Tazapay acquisition to close in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. Circle Ventures had led Tazapay's $36 million Series B extension in March. Binance also bought $100 million worth of Circle shares in September and signed a new five-year USDC agreement.
