#5050. I Didn't Expect to Love This Prada Cologne. But This Is Why It's My Go-To Fall Scent

Prada Paradigme looks loud. The cologne inside is surprisingly refined.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHEN PRADA PARADIGME Eau de Parfum was released last year, the first thing I noticed was the bottle. It has a stark lime-green-and-black design that can best be described as Green Goblin chic, which is ironic considering Spider-Man himself, Tom Holland, fronts its campaign. The fragrance itself, however, is no joke. I dug the scent so much, I quickly featured it at the top of my next new releases column before giving it a 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award.

Prada clearly felt similarly, as it dropped a more concentrated Prada Paradigme Le Parfum this May. After wearing the OG cologne regularly for over a year, I can confirm my early impression of it wasn’t t misguided. Here’s how the Eau de Parfum performed over 12 months and how the new Le Parfum stacks up.

At its core, Paradigme is an amber-woody cologne, which is definitely up my alley. But it’s also bold and spicy—two cologne descriptors I tend to avoid. Paradigme pulls off hitting this intersection of vibes with a scent profile that is refined and powerful yet still grounded and casual.

It opens with a warm blend of Peru balsam, benzoin resin, and guaiac wood before settling into a musky finish with some hints of citrusy bergamot and rose. There’s also a lingering bourbon note that I especially appreciate as someone who loves the smell (and taste) of whiskey. In the Le Parfum, the citrus and floral notes come through a bit clearer and definitely stick around longer. But it has the same rich amber-woody base.

To me, this is ideal for wear at a low-lit cocktail bar, that’s potentially haunted in the best possible way. In short, this is what I’d wear if I was hitting up Overlook Hotel’s bar in Stephen King’s The Shining—not to be confused with the Stanley Hotel in Colorado, on which that hotel is based, which I have visited and wore something lighter at (it’s pretty tight in there). Prada Paradigme Le Parfum, on the other hand, is better suited for wandering around the Overlook’s extensive hedge maze.

This more concentrated iteration is best suited for spring and summer, as its deeper floral notes could clash with the cozy vibe of fall and winter. While the EDP is best-suited for the cooler, moodier months, I dig it when temps are high too. There’s enough bergamot and rose in there to reflect the brightness of the season, and the guaiac wood gives it a slight earthy edge that works well during the warmer months. I’m also someone who gladly enjoys sipping on bourbon when it’s 90 degrees out, so my view may be skewed.

After applying the cologne with two to three sprays to my neck, I get about eight to nine hours of quality wear. The Le Parfum lasts about an hour longer and maintains its intensity more strongly than the EDP. It also builds more in intensity over the first couple of hours before plateauing, whereas the EDP settles after about 45 minutes and stays consistent for the next few hours. I usually stick to two sprays with the Le Parfum, as the projection is stronger.

Prada Paradigme Eau de Parfum strikes a rare balance between bold and easygoing, blending amber woods, spice, bergamot, rose, and bourbon. It feels refined without being stuffy, works across seasons, and lasts roughly eight to nine hours on my skin—making it an easy everyday fragrance with enough personality for nights out. If you’re looking for something stronger and slightly spicier, Prada Paradigme Le Parfum is the pick. It lasts longer, but the scent isn’t as well-suited for year-round wear as the OG.

USDC Issuer Circle Quietly Cuts 5% of Staff in Profitable Quarter

Circle, the company behind the USDC stablecoin, has cut about 5% of its workforce, according to its third-quarter earnings release on Wednesday.

The reduction was "designed to better align our organizational structure with our operating model and strategic priorities," the company said in footnotes to its financial tables. Circle did not say how many employees were affected or which teams were cut.

It recorded $9.1 million in restructuring expenses in the quarter, mostly cash payments for notice periods and severance, employee benefits and related costs. Those were partly offset by a $5.7 million reversal of stock-based compensation, as unvested shares held by departing employees were forfeited.

The cuts came in a profitable quarter. Circle reported net income from continuing operations of $226 million, up 5% from a year earlier, on total revenue and reserve income of $865 million, up 17%. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 85% year-on-year to $317 million.

Much of that growth came from outside Circle's core business. Other revenue rose to $207 million, including $182 million from the presale of ARC, the token for its Arc blockchain. Reserve income, the interest Circle earns on the assets backing USDC and its largest source of revenue, fell 8% to $658 million as interest rates on those reserves declined.

The average amount of USDC in circulation rose 8% from a year earlier to $73.3 billion, but ended the quarter flat at $73.9 billion. USDC's share of the U.S. dollar stablecoin market slipped to 27%, according to the company.

CEO Jeremy Allaire did not mention the job cuts in his comments on the results, or in a tweet on Wednesday calling Q3 "a big quarter for Circle." He said USDC carried 79% of all stablecoin transaction volume, up from 66% a year earlier, and that Circle's payments network ended the quarter at $41 billion in annualized volume, up 15-fold. "In January, the GENIUS Act takes effect and regulated digital dollars go mainstream," Allaire wrote. "Every layer of our platform is live and ready for it."

→ USDC carried 79% of all stablecoin transaction volume, up from 66% a year ago, and $13.9T moved onchain (+49%)

→ A record $208B of USDC was minted and redeemed, about $2.3B every day

→ Arc mainnet went live, with 100+ institutions and apps… pic.twitter.com/euVfyHBUXX

— Jeremy Allaire (@jerallaire) November 4, 2026

The cuts come as Circle expands. In September, it launched the public mainnet of its Arc blockchain, with BlackRock, DTCC and Visa among its permissioned validators. Allaire said in October that Circle plans to enter about 40 emerging and developing markets, and the company has since teamed up with payments-technology firm ACI Worldwide to pilot USDC settlement on Colombia's instant-payments network.

Circle is the latest in a string of crypto companies to cut staff this year, citing weaker markets, artificial intelligence or both.

Coinbase cut 14% of its workforce in May, with CEO Brian Armstrong pointing to the crypto downturn and the company's adoption of AI. The Ethereum Foundation cut 20% of its staff in June as part of a reorganization, while custody firm BitGo cut 15% that month to focus on AI and stablecoins.

Exchange Luno cut a fifth of its global staff in July, citing automation, and crypto ETF issuer Bitwise cut 14% of its staff in August.

#5047. Researchers Used an Old Treatment from the ‘70s to Help Alzheimer’s Patients. The Results Were Shocking.

There are a lot of treatments in development for people with Alzheimer's disease, but new research is exploring an unusual tactic that hails back to the '70s. It's called external counterpulsation (ECP), and it's a special treatment that uses squeezable cuffs to compress the lower body.

The study, which was published in the American Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease & Other Dementias, found that patients with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer's disease gained several points on cognitive scales after using ECP, suggesting it may be a promising therapy worth further investigation.

The ECP contraption looks similar to compression boots that have become trendy, with a few important differences. This device extends higher to include the butt, calves, and thighs, and also inflates and deflates with the person’s cardiac cycle. Regular compression boots do not. And, while it seems random that a tool like this might help to improve memory, neurologists who treat patients with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease say there may be something to this news.

Meet the experts: Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California; Liron Sinvani, MD, director of research and innovation for the Institute for Healthy Aging at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research; and Anna Hohler, MD, regional director of Neurology for Westchester, Northwell Health, and chair of Neurology for Northern Westchester and Phelps hospitals.

For the study, researchers recruited 190 people with early Alzheimer's disease to participate in a 12-month randomized controlled trial. Participants were either given three to five weekly one-hour ECP sessions for 35 treatments or a sham treatment that exerted much less pressure. After that, they received treatments twice a week through six months. Participants went through cognitive assessments at the start of the study, and also at weeks 6, 12, 18, 24, 36, and 52.

After analyzing the data, researchers discovered that people who went through the ECP treatments had improvements in cognition, including memory, attention, language, and reasoning. They also seemed to do better at doing everyday tasks like getting dressed, eating, and doing household tasks. They continued to have cognitive benefits even after they were done receiving the treatments.

However, there are “important reasons to be cautious” about the results, says Liron Sinvani, MD, director of research and innovation for the Institute for Healthy Aging at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research, noting that the research was funded by the company that makes the ECP device used in the study, and that the lead author works for the same company.

Doctors say that one possible explanation behind these results is the boost in blood flow that comes with this compression therapy.

"External counterpulsation is thought to improve blood flow throughout the body, including to the brain," explains Anna Hohler, MD, regional director of Neurology for Westchester, Northwell Health, and chair of Neurology for Northern Westchester and Phelps hospitals. "Because reduced cerebral blood flow has been associated with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease, enhancing circulation may help support brain function and potentially improve memory and attention in some patients with early-stage disease."

Dr. Sinvani agrees. "The rationale for ECP makes biological sense: By improving blood flow to the brain, enhancing vascular function, reducing inflammation, and potentially improving the brain's ability to clear toxic proteins, ECP may address a critical and often overlooked piece of the Alzheimer's puzzle," she says.

In general, "what is healthy for your heart is usually healthy for your brain, and what is unhealthy for your heart is usually unhealthy for your brain," says Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California.

That's unclear. "I think it could, and this trial makes a compelling case for why it deserves further investigation," Dr. Sinvani says. She praises ECP's non-invasive nature and well-established safety profile as being big perks of this technology. “It is essentially a passive cardiovascular workout,” she says.

"While the early findings are intriguing, larger studies are needed before this therapy can be widely recommended for Alzheimer's disease," Dr. Hohler says. "If future research confirms meaningful cognitive benefits and long-term safety, external counterpulsation could become a useful adjunctive treatment, particularly because it is noninvasive and already has an established safety record in cardiovascular care."

There are treatment options available for people diagnosed with early Alzheimer's disease. These include FDA-approved medications to slow progression of the disease, therapies for symptoms, cognitive stimulation, physical exercise, good sleep hygiene, management of vascular risk factors, and social engagement, Dr. Hohler says.

"A comprehensive approach that combines medical treatment with healthy lifestyle interventions currently offers the best opportunity to preserve cognitive function and quality of life," she says.

Democrats have won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections, giving the party greater influence over legislation and oversight of President Donald Trump’s administration.

#5045. The 10 Best Hiking Backpacks, Tested by Outdoor Gear Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

We tested dozens of packs and found Osprey’s Kestrel LT 45 to be the best.

A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear. Whether you're venturing deep into the backcountry or exploring a local trail, your pack will be strapped to your back for an extended period of time. It needs to be reliable, comfortable, durable, and offer the right storage and organization options to suit your style of hiking. Oh, and affordability is a nice-to-have, too.

Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress. Backpack technology isn't what it used to be when your grandpappy was hitting the trail. It's far better but also a lot more complicated. You'll need to understand frame types and nylon fabric densities and hydration system compatibilities and—well, you get the picture. It's all just a little more confusing than it needs to be. That's why our expert team put together this guide to the best hiking backpacks to help you find the perfect pack without breaking your back and the bank in the process.

As an outdoors writer, I spend countless weeks outside each year. During that time, I've put the most popular and well-reviewed hiking backpacks to the test to determine the best of the best. Over the last 12 months, I've tested dozens of packs from Mystery Ranch, Gossamer Gear, Gregory, Osprey, and more throughout the U.S., in Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of New Hampshire, the vast deserts of Big Bend National Park, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking backpacks, I've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, ease of packing, weight, durability, how well (or not) the weight is spread throughout, and how much gear can fit in them.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or a full-fledged expedition pack for tackling the wilds of Patagonia, we've got you covered with the 10 best hiking backpacks for any trail.

Winner of this year’s “Best New All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one. It’s Osprey’s reimagining of the classic rucksack design. It’s rugged yet lightweight, with a 45-liter capacity that’s more than enough for most hikers on all but the longest multiday treks. I personally love the streamlined exterior that cinches down tight for maximum compression. Osprey’s AirScape back panel offers just-right cushioning, coupled with simple torso-length adjustability to fit a wide range of body shapes and sizes.

After months of testing, this has consistently proven to be my go-to pack for most hikes because everything about it just works. Plus, the price point hits the midrange sweet spot, ensuring it’s affordable enough for most, even for first-time hiking backpack buyers on a budget. Bonus: An attached rain cover is included.

At just 12 liters and weighing only 390 grams, this pack is designed for ultra-efficient climbs and lightning-fast summit assaults. It's the daypack you grab when most other daypacks are too much. I found the simple organizational layout—one main compartment and two zippered pockets (one internal, one external)—made wrangling my day hiking essentials a breeze. Additional gear loops at the rear provide extra space for hanging anything you might need at the ready. The just-right back padding, removable hip belt, and ventilated mesh shoulder straps were extremely comfy for tackling daily summits in the White Mountains.

It's all made from recycled, eco-friendly materials that are Bluesign certified, with a PFC-free DWR treatment. The best part? It's among the most affordable brand-name speedpacks we'd recommend this year.

Like every Gregory pack I've tested in the last two decades, the Paragon 60 is durable, cleverly designed, and features smart organizational options. But I'm including it here mainly because it's so dang comfy to wear. It features a widely adjustable torso length and an airy mesh back panel that breathes well thanks to a design that's 90 percent air. The hip belt is equally adjustable, too, with dynamic panels that move independently of the frame. Translation: It's the most comfortable pack I tested this year, even after hundreds of miles of hiking with fairly heavy loads.

Bonus: The PFAS-free durable water-repellent (DWR) coating on the body, bottom, and pack lining means it's more eco-friendly, too.

Yeti’s first foray into the hardcore hiking backpack game comes on the heels of its recent acquisition of the Mystery Ranch brand. The Skala is a deft combination of Mystery Ranch’s legendary design prowess and Yeti’s built-to-survive-anything durability. The former’s RipZip opening is the star of this pack, providing instant access to its contents with a quick one-handed pull. The Skala features multiple adjustment points and a clever load distribution system that combine to ensure a perfect fit and all-day comfort on the trail.

True to the Yeti brand, it's packed with premium, heavy-duty materials built to survive years of abuse. The only downsides? At 3.4 pounds, it’s heavier than many in this weight class. It’s also pricier than most of its competition. But if you’re a fan of Yeti and/or MR and don’t mind the “buy once, cry once” price point, this is definitely worth considering.

For an all-in-one solution—a backpack that moves effortlessly from your morning commute to the office to the trail and back again—Peak Design's new Outdoor 25L pack delivers. The frameless, low-profile build is extremely comfy on and off the trail. The brand's signature organizational elements are here, too—it's hydration system-compatible, features a 16-inch laptop sleeve, and is purpose-built to accept PD's own gear cubes (sold separately) so you can divvy up the main compartment however you see fit. The drawstring/roll-top closure provides quick and easy access to the internal compartment while protecting your gear from the elements. Fair warning, though: You'll pay a premium for the PD brand name. If you’re looking to size up, the Outdoor Backpack is also available as a more generous 45-liter option.

Mountain Hardwear is upending the ultralight backpacking game with the debut of the all-new Alakazam series. The 45-liter model won a coveted spot in this year’s Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. At just 820 grams, it’s absurdly lightweight with a trail-friendly fit that feels like wearing nothing at all. Yet, it offers enough room for both gear-heavy day hikes and overnights. It’s all thanks to the bleeding-edge ALUULA shell fabric, which is not only light but extremely durable. The storage and organization (with plenty of loops, pockets, and oversized stash pouches) are cleverly laid out, and the unique GiddyUp compression system allows you to cinch your load down on the go. I also especially love the roll-top design that makes the entire bag waterproof. (A 60-liter option is also available.)

Like many Arc'teryx packs, the Alpha FL30 is first and foremost built for climbing (including a top strap, six lash points, and a built-in RECCO reflector for SAR situations). But, I also found its sleek silhouette and featherweight construction great for fast-packing. It's only as heavy as it needs to be while still protecting your gear with the brand's own abrasion-resistant Hadron grid fabric. The drawstring opening provides quick access to a cavernous, open-concept interior with only a single, small zippered security pocket.

It's a no-frills design with minimal organization options that won't please every hiker. But it's a solid, if pricey, option for hard-charging trail lovers who appreciate a pack that stays out of its own way.

With a 44-liter capacity, the Talon 44 is large enough for two-day weekender trips and even longer multiday treks. It's an ideal bag for most hikers looking to buy just one backpack that does it all. I love the slim profile, excellent padding, and close-to-body fit—all of which makes for more comfortable wear, especially after long days on the trail.

This iteration of Osprey's best-seller features a long list of upgrades to the straps, padding, and overall design. Plus, I found the sheer number of storage options to be perfect for almost any length of trip.

I’ve been a fan of Gossamer Gear’s featherweight fastpacker-friendly gear for years. The Grit 28 is my go-to for fast day hikes and quick summit assaults where I’m willing to trade comfort and convenience for speed. At just over a pound, the 28-liter pack is streamlined and sized right. The storage options are limited, ensuring you pack only what you need and nothing more.

What sets it apart from most of its competition is the vest-style shoulder and sternum straps that wear more like a racing vest for maximum all-day comfort. Despite its light weight, it’s made from two ultra-durable fabrics that I’ve found stand up to plenty of trail abuse.

The Crossroads 27L Carry-On is, first and foremost, a travel backpack (it fits under most airline seats, making it a great carry-on backpack). But Yeti bakes in plenty of trail-ready durability to make this one good enough for hiking, too. The 700-denier TuffSkin Nylon exterior is both water- and abrasion-resistant, with an extra durable and easy-to-clean PU-coated base. Contoured, EVA-foam shoulder straps and a no-pressure back panel make for easy carrying, even during long layovers.

Plus, with a suspended laptop sleeve and multiple zippered pockets inside and out, this has become my go-to weekender bag, especially on trips where I'm intent on hitting the trail straight from the airport. (Pro tip: Pair it with Yeti's own Crossroads packing cubes for maximum organization options.)

Ultimately, every hiking backpack is designed for hauling "stuff." The amount of stuff each pack can carry—its capacity—is measured in liters (L) or cubic inches. The right size for you depends on how long you typically hike for (hours, days, weeks?) and how heavy a packer you are. If you're shopping for your first pack, finding the perfect capacity can involve a little trial and error. But for a wide variety of hikers, the following numbers are a good starting point.

If you tend to pack light, the right capacity for you may fall closer to the lower end of the above ranges. If you're an over-packer (no shame!), consider sizing up to a slightly larger pack with a capacity on the upper end of the above ranges. Again: Trial and error.

You may have heard an old hiker's adage that goes something like, "Ounces make pounds, and pounds make pain." It's a simple axiom, but it's true: The more weight you carry, the more work you need to do on the trail. That's why it's important to pack as light as possible while still taking all the essentials. It helps to start with as light a hiking backpack as you can afford. The difference between three pounds and four pounds might not seem like much when you're standing in your living room, but I promise you'll feel every gram of that one-pound difference after 10 miles.

There are three main types of backpack construction: internal frame, external frame, and frameless. External frame packs have largely been phased out in the mainstream outdoor gear space in favor of internal frame models. True to the name, they feature a rigid structure that's "hidden" inside the pack's back panel. They sit closer to the back, hugging the body for a more streamlined fit that's ultimately more comfortable. All but the smallest hiking backpacks we recommend below rely on an internal frame construction.

Some compact daypacks (usually 20 liters or less) use a frameless construction similar to standard school backpacks. The lack of a frame means they're not ideal for supporting heavier loads, but that typically isn't an issue if you're only carrying enough for an afternoon hike. Without a frame, most of these packs collapse down almost completely flat, making them perfect travel backpacks.

Some packs—particularly those designed for alpine climbers—rely on top-loading-only designs. Think of a typical shopping bag where the contents are only accessible directly through the top opening. It's simple but limiting. Thankfully, many of the best hiking backpacks these days are accessible via both top and side openings. For larger packs, this makes it infinitely easier to get to the gear at the bottom of your pack without having to take everything out first.

The "best" storage layout is personal to each hiker. If you're an organizational nerd (I count myself among this camp), you may prefer more pockets to better wrangle your gear in a way that makes sense to you. On the other end of the spectrum are alpine-style bags that typically trade more pockets (and zippers and stitching) for a simpler, lighter-weight design. These tend to feature a single open-concept storage compartment with only one or two smaller storage pockets.

A few pieces of gear you want to pack in your hiking backpack include: a hydration bladder, water bottle(s), a phone (with easy access to its camera), a satellite messenger, and bear spray. Most modern bags also offer external storage options, like reinforced crampon patches and gear loops or "daisy chains" (i.e., webbing stitched into the pack's exterior that provides multiple attachment points for wet gear, ice axes, helmets, and more that you may not want to store inside your pack).

Modern hiking backpacks can be deceptively complex, and there are dozens of technical features available on many of today's best models. If you're shopping for anything other than a daypack, consider a bag with a dedicated sleeping bag compartment and sleeping pad straps. For longer treks where you may want to venture away from base camp once you set up your tent, a removable daypack (sometimes the "brain" or top lid of a larger pack converts into an ultra-compact hip bag for this purpose), and a rain cover, which may be a stand-alone piece of fabric with a stretch seam or sewn into the pack itself, so you can easily pull it over the pack if the weather turns south.

#5043. This New Treatment Duo Could Halt Grays and Make Hair Thicker

Clinical trial results have some interesting findings.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

GRAY HAIR IS A NORMAL PART of life for plenty of people, but not everyone feels comfortable embracing their inner Andie MacDowell. While solutions to cover up grays have largely been limited to finding a colorist you love, a new study confirms there's a product that could stop new silver strands from forming.

It's called The System by Arey, and a new clinical trial published in the current issue of Journal of Drugs in Dermatology suggests there could be something to it. The System, which is a supplement and serum duo, aims to tackle the reasons people form grays that have nothing to do with genetics, like nutrition and oxidative stress.

Meet the experts: Joshua Zeichner, MD, is director of cosmetic and clinical research at The Mount Sinai Hospital. Gary Goldenberg, MD, is assistant clinical professor of dermatology at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Hospital. Jay Small, trichologist, is celebrity hairstylist, and co-founder of Arey. Cindy Wassef, MD, is a dermatologist at Premier Health Associates in Randolph, New Jersey.

Dermatologists are skeptical—and say hair dye may still be your strongest option. But the new clinical trial results suggest there's something to consider here. Here's what the trial found, plus why this treatment duo could work.

The study authors recruited 173 men and women between the ages of 18 and 65 who had not dyed their hair for at least a month. Participants were randomized into four groups: Those who used The System, those who took the supplement and a placebo serum, those who used the serum and took a placebo supplement, and people who used a placebo supplement and serum. Participants were followed for 26 weeks, with regular visits and check-ins to make sure they were still following their prescribed treatment. The researchers also took photos of the participants' hair during the visits.

Researchers discovered that people who used The System had a "progressive decrease" in the amount of gray hairs they had at weeks 12 and 24. Specifically, they had 9 percent less grays at week 12 and 13 percent less grays at week 24. People in the placebo group, on the other hand, saw their grays increase by 10 percent during the 24-week study. At the end of the 24 week trial, 88 percent of subjects in the combination group had less gray hairs or no increase in grays, while only 12 percent had more gray hair. But 35 percent of those in the placebo group had more grays by week 24.

The participants who used The System also reported that their hair was three times thicker, fuller, and shinier than those who took a placebo. "To our knowledge, this is the first randomized, controlled, double-blind clinical trial on the novel use of a combination of an oral supplement and a topical serum on grey hair," the researchers wrote.

Your hair can go gray from a range of things, including nutritional deficiencies, oxidative, stress, simple aging, and genetics. "A lack of certain key nutrients like copper, iron, Vitamin B12, and Vitamin D3 deprives the follicles of the essential cofactors needed to sustain cellular energy and continuous melanin synthesis," says Jay Small, trichologist, celebrity hairstylist, and co-founder of Arey.

Other elements like daily UV exposure, harsh chemicals in your haircare products, and pollution can cause oxidative stress, leading to dull, ashy hair that turns gray and then white, Small adds. The System tries to address nutritional deficiencies, while supporting growth and circulation from the outside.

While Small says people usually assume that genetics is the main reason they go gray, he says the study "proves that when diet and lifestyle factors are addressed, a majority of us can slow down accelerated hair aging."

Dermatologists agree that you can go gray from a range of factors. "A depletion of melanocyte stem cells—cells that make color—in the hair follicle reduces melanin, the actual color," confirms Gary Goldenberg, MD, assistant clinical professor of dermatology at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Hospital. "Oxidative stress, smoking, UV exposure, nutritional deficiencies, thyroid disease, and general stress also contribute to this process."

Gray hair has also been linked with a decrease in an enzyme called catalase, which is known to break down hydrogen peroxide in the hair follicle that is thought to be the cause of graying, according to Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research at The Mount Sinai Hospital. "Various topical treatments and oral supplements have been brought to the market and are aimed at this pathway," he says. "While they may offer some benefit, none have proven to be the cure we are looking for."

Again, people can go gray for a range of reasons and it's hard to say in any given situation why your hair lost its pigment. "We know at least some of the causes of hair graying—the Arey system aims to address some of these known factors," says Cindy Wassef, MD, a dermatologist at Premier Health Associates in Randolph, New Jersey. "If it is playing a role in the graying of hair for that particular person, it is possible that they will notice less grey hair production." Basically, if your hair is graying for environmental or nutritional reasons, this may help; If it’s due to genetics, it’s unlikely to do much.

An important caveat to keep in mind is that once hair has already gone gray, Dr. Zeichner says it's "extremely unlikely" that it will repigment, or go back to its original color.

Arey's The System is available online now. If you're interested, you can try it. Just be aware that it's not guaranteed to work, especially since it's hard to know exactly what's fueling your grays. "The good news is that if these products aren’t helping your grays, you can always find a good hair colorist," Dr. Zeichner says.

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. #5042. Bitcoin Shrugs Off Midterms as Experts Say Democratic Sweep Was 'Priced In'

Bitcoin Shrugs Off Midterms as Experts Say Democratic Sweep Was 'Priced In'

Democrats flipped both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the U.S. midterms, handing President Donald Trump a major political setback.

Experts say this was not the "preferred outcome" for crypto markets and that it has increased "uncertainty" for future pro-crypto policy. However, after a brief dip, Bitcoin is up 1.6% over the past 24 hours and now sits at $78,277, per Decrypt data. Broadly, almost every top 100 crypto token by market cap is in the green for the day.

"I think the Democratic sweep was largely priced in going into the midterms," André Dragosch, head of research at Bitwise Europe, told Decrypt. "The downside risks were fairly limited going into these midterms as sentiment was already very bearish and there were already signs of seller exhaustion again. So, it is no surprise that we have seen this kind of V-shaped recovery on an intraday basis during the midterms."

Polymarket put odds of the Democratic Party sweeping both the House and Senate during the midterms at 65.5% at the start of the week. Dragosch said these odds meant that markets weren't shocked by Tuesday's results.

James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares, agreed. "My sense is that Bitcoin had largely priced in a Democratic sweep, leaving room for a relief rally as uncertainty clears," he said in comments shared with Decrypt. "Therefore, the anticipated result need not trigger another sell-off."

"Crypto policy did not decide the midterms. The economy, gas prices, the Iran situation, and Trump's unmet promises did," Heslin Kim, co-founder and CBO of Zenith, told Decrypt. "Crypto policy was irrelevant to the broader voting pool, but it now has the baggage of all the egregious activity that was stirred up in our ecosystem associated with the Trump family."

Tim Sun, senior analyst at HashKey, told Decrypt that the results do "increase the uncertainty surrounding the progress of crypto policy," but that Bitcoin's price action means that the market doesn't interpret it as a "major negative catalyst."

Specifically, this may be because the midterm results don't mean the Democrats can roll back existing pro-crypto guidelines set out by the SEC and CFTC, Dragosch said. However, it does mean that going forward, the market cannot rely as heavily on Trump's "political tailwinds for momentum," Sun added.

It also complicates the picture for the Clarity Act, which would establish rules for crypto markets. The bill has been in limbo since it was introduced in 2025, with many Democrats opposing it due to Trump's crypto conflicts of interest.

Dmitry Machikhin, CEO of BitOK, predicted in a note shared with Decrypt that the Clarity Act will remain in limbo well into 2027, thanks to the midterm results.

"The greater concern is slower crypto reform," Butterfill said. "CLARITY faces a harder path, while investigations into Trump-linked ventures could consume political capital and generate uncomfortable headlines across the sector. But the administration remains in place, and existing regulatory progress, including GENIUS, does not simply disappear."

He expects U.S. exchanges, token issuers and businesses that rely on new regulatory permissions to be more sensitive to the result than Bitcoin, and said established, compliant operators could even gain if scrutiny falls disproportionately on weaker competitors.

"A Democratic Congress may even be good for the industry in one way," Marcin Kaźmierczak, co-founder and COO of RedStone, told Decrypt. "Crypto shouldn't depend on one political camp. Infrastructure has to work for whoever is in power and bring most value to the ecosystem participants. Finance is changing, and politics will not stop it."

Despite the switch-up in the House and Senate, Dragosch expects little to change over the next two years.

"I personally expect more disputes, disagreements, and simply more of 'nothing stops this train,'" he said, pointing to a lack of significant progress to rein in fiscal deficits. "We will probably remain in a fiscally dominant environment with increasing fiscal risks, which I think is ultimately a tailwind for hard assets like Bitcoin."

Instead, he believes macro factors "remain in the driver's seat for now." Specifically, he points to a potential upcoming pivot from the Federal Reserve as a response to "increasing risk" around the AI trade.

"This will likely cause renewed interest in debasement-resistant assets like Bitcoin," Dragosch said, "and will continue to drive institutional adoption via ETPs and treasury companies as well."

Butterfill also pointed to macro factors. "For Bitcoin, real yields, dollar liquidity and ETP flows still carry more weight than the elections," he said. "I would temper expectations for the pace of U.S. reform, while remaining constructive on institutional adoption. How Trump responds to being constrained is the less predictable part."

Rep. Hill has led the House Financial Services Committee for the past two years, during which members passed the first federal framework for stablecoins as well as a sweeping crypto bill.

As of Wednesday afternoon, House Financial Services Committee Chair French Hill's race for reelection is too close to call as a Democratic takeover in the House is set to usher in a new slate of leaders and reshape the future of crypto legislation in Congress.

On Tuesday night into Wednesday, Hill has been neck and neck with Democratic candidate Chris Jones in Arkansas, according to the Associated Press, with 99% of votes already reported. Hill held a slim lead at publication time.

Hill has led the House Financial Services Committee for the past two years, during which members passed the first federal framework for stablecoins as well as a sweeping crypto bill. Crypto political action committee Fairshake and other PACs spent $1 million on Hill's campaign, according to reporting from the Arkansas Democrat Gazette.

Other crypto-friendly lawmakers also secured reelection, including Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y., and current House Agriculture Committee Chair Glenn "GT" Thompson, R-Pa. Later in the day on Wednesday, Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-MI., who is viewed favorably by the crypto industry, lost his seat to Democratic candidate Sean McCann, according to the Associated Press.

Candidate Shomari Figures beat Republican candidate Rhett Marques in Alabama. Figures was endorsed by crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto, given his vote on sweeping digital asset legislation called the Clarity Act.

With the House flipping control, Democrats will usher in the agenda for key congressional committees that have jurisdiction over crypto and prediction markets. Top Democrat Maxine Waters will likely take back her spot as House Financial Services Committee chair, leaving Hill out of his top spot, but likely to be the top Republican on that committee.

#5039. Bitcoin rebounds past $80,000 as markets shrug off midterms and Binance hack

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Ether jumped nearly 6% and crypto stocks rallied, while Bitwise says the market’s muted reaction to the Binance hack shows growing maturity.

Bitcoin has recovered from its post-Binance hack losses, surging toward $81,000 following Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, which saw Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress.

"Markets took the Democratic win in stride," Nexo analysts wrote in their daily dispatch. "Futures fell as much as 2.5% on early counts and then recovered fully, which suggests investors saw the outcome as adding clarity and not as changing the growth story."

Bitcoin (BTC) was up 3.5% to $80,500 on Wednesday afternoon, while Ethereum jumped nearly 6% to $2,433. Solana and XRP were up a more muted 2.5% on the day.

Futures data suggests traders are adjusting existing positions rather than taking on additional leverage, according to Nexo. Crypto futures volume climbed 27%, while open interest rose just 3%, and Bitcoin open interest grew more slowly than its price. Roughly $469 million in leveraged positions were also flushed out.

Nexo said market orders have shifted to a slight net buying bias after favoring sellers the previous day, while the most actively traded Bitcoin options are predominantly calls.

Crypto-related stocks also rallied, with Strategy and Coinbase gaining about 6% each; Strategy's variable-rate perpetual preferred stock STRC hit $100 for the first time since May.

"The case for holding Bitcoin crosses party lines," Executive Chairman Michael Saylor said earlier Wednesday.

Block Inc. jumped 15% following its earnings report, while bitcoin treasury firm Strive climbed roughly 12%. Meanwhile, the Official Trump (TRUMP) memecoin fell 17%.

Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan argued that the market's relatively muted reaction to the Binance hack reflects the crypto industry's growing maturity and improved security infrastructure.

In his weekly blog memo, Hougan examined the 10 largest crypto-related hacks in history and found that Bitcoin finished higher in the following 30 days in five cases and lower in five, suggesting no consistent relationship between major security incidents and Bitcoin's subsequent performance.

He said Bitcoin's roughly 4% decline following the Binance breach was largely in line with broader risk assets, emphasizing that Binance was hacked, not the Bitcoin network.

"Hacks would impact the market if they suggested there is no safer way to hold bitcoin, but there is. In this case, the stolen crypto was held in online hot wallets at a large, integrated crypto exchange," Hougan wrote.

He pointed to institutional custodians, cold storage and spot Bitcoin ETFs as increasingly secure alternatives for investors, highlighting ETFs in particular because their underlying assets are held in offline cold storage and subject to multiple withdrawal approvals and restrictions.

Hougan's assessment was echoed by Matt Mena, crypto research strategist at 21Shares, who said the market's resilience following the Binance breach was encouraging.

"What we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it," Mena wrote in a Tuesday report. "The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke: banks, payment networks, and asset managers kept shipping onchain products through the drawdown, and regulators kept writing rules."

Mena is watching four things into November: whether Bitcoin holds $76,000 to $78,000 and sustains its move back above $80,000 to $82,000; Binance's progress in completing withdrawals and proving its reserves; credit spreads, oil prices, and long-end Treasury yields; and whether ETF inflows return.

#5038. Puking, Passing, Posting: The New Rules of Race Etiquette

More athletes than ever are showing up to starting lines of all kinds.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Race etiquette used to be pretty straightforward: Stay in your lane, don’t cut people off, and be aware of your surroundings when you stop for water. But ever since run clubs and new hybrid competitions like Hyrox have taken off, there's been an influx of athletes who have never been taught race rules. To make matters more complicated, new competition styles mean additional rules have to get ironed out in real time. Best case scenario, this might mean you bump into a few people with cameras trying to get social media content at the finish line. Worst case scenario (in rare, extreme cases), the race may turn into a literal sh*tshow.

“Racing has become much more popularized and mainstream over the years, bringing in more people who may be racing from more of a ‘fun’ standpoint rather than a competitive one,” says kettlebell coach Sarah Warshowsky, CPT, creator of the WH Build & Burn kettlebell plan who’s competed in a Hyrox race and half-marathon. “Newer racers need to respect the history, competition, and elite athletes who may have prize money on the line, while competitive racers should feel inclusive and accepting of new racers coming into their sport because in the end, it does bring more eyes to it.”

Meet the experts: Sarah Warshowsky, CPT, is a New York City–based kettlebell coach and creator of the Build & Burn kettlebell track. Kayla Jeter, CFSC, is a Lululemon athlete, wellness consultant, and veteran half-, full, and ultramarathoner. Sunny Choi, CSCS, is an Olympic breaker who’s competed in a Hyrox race.

Knowing all the ins and outs of how to act during a race isn’t exactly part of your ChatGPT training plan, but race etiquette is essential. That’s why Women’s Health tapped some of our most trusted racing experts to put together a comprehensive list of the new rules of race etiquette—here’s what to know before you head to the starting line.

Be respectful and practice spatial awareness, both when you’re maintaining a steady pace, and passing people. After all, “the point of a race is that you want to pass people and you want people to feel like they can pass you,” says Warshowsky. But you need to check your surroundings, and be strategic about when you can make those passes. For instance, if you’re about to turn a corner down a new street during a half-marathon, you might want to wait a second before you try and squeeze past a bunch of people.

Similarly, some races like Hyrox also have passing lanes for faster athletes. Do your event research ahead of time, know which lane you’re in, keep it moving, and if you need to switch, look around and try not to knock into runners, Warshowsky says.

After all, it’s your race too! “Too many times, I’ve experienced and seen others almost fall from ‘me’-centric runners moving erratically,” says Kayla Jeter, CFSC, a Lululemon athlete, wellness consultant, and veteran half-, full, and ultramarathoner. “If someone starts swerving, I’ll casually start snapping to announce my presence, I’ll also use my arms as a barrier to keep people from bumping into me.”

If you’re in desperate need of water or a walking break, stay on the lookout for an upcoming water station or less crowded area to stop by. Just like you would when riding a bike, stick out your hand to the right or left to signify that you’ll be pulling over, Warshowsky says. Then, start inching your way toward that side of the road “instead of needing to cut across an entire lane of people running,” she adds. If you need a walking break, raise your arm straight up in the air before slowing down.

“Go into every race knowing you’re not the only one on the course and are responsible for how your actions impact someone else’s race,” Jeter reminds. So, if you want to record content, do your best not to include people in the background, whether you’re at the start line, finish line, or mile 10. Want to stop and grab a couple of videos? Look around you and make sure no one is right behind you. “I’ve seen plenty of runners crash into someone crossing the finish line because someone wanted to capture their moment,” she adds.

Ultimately, just be respectful. “A creator filming themselves having their own experience does not have to bother anyone around them, as long as they are not coming in the way of anyone else's experience,” says Warshowsky.

Understand the guidelines and your race order ahead of time. At Hyrox, the stations are numbered pretty clearly, but if you get lost, don’t be afraid to ask a nearby judge for help, says Warshowsky.

After finishing up at one of the machines, participants don’t typically wipe sweat off after leaving it since that can take time off of their score. But you should make sure the station is relatively clean and the weights are in place so you’re not putting the person behind you at a major disadvantage, she adds.

PRing your race is not worth ignoring a bodily emergency. Before getting to the start line, know the nearest exits and bathrooms in each section of the race, Warshowsky says. Then, “if you have any signs of discomfort, listen to your body, because those signs are usually not there for nothing,” says Olympic breaker Sunny Choi, CSCS, who has competed in a Hyrox race. Hit the nearest bathroom, and if you don’t make it, try to find a nearby empty space to stay in until you feel better.

If you start feeling faint during Hyrox or something more serious may be going on but you still have four more stations to go, don’t power through. Tell a volunteer or someone working the course that you may need medical attention. “The only way that you can get help is if you let someone know you actually need help,” Warshowsky adds. “The safety of yourself and others around you should be number-one priority when needing to make the call whether you need to exit the race for any reason.”

Nothing New on Race Day!When it comes to clothing and sneakers, “as tempting as it can be to wear something fresh at the start line, new products are often stiff, which can cause chaffing and be distracting,” says Jeter. The same goes for food: New fuel mixed with nerves may make your stomach feel weird at an inconvenient time during the race, Choi adds. So, make sure you know what feels best in your body pre-race day by testing it ahead of time, like during a taper run.

When you’re running in the middle of the street and you have a water cup in one hand and an energy gel in the other, pulling to the side to throw them in the trash is probably not top of mind. But throwing trash anywhere on the ground can cause it to get trapped underneath athletes’ feet and potentially cause tripping. (Plus, it’s more trash for the people cleaning up afterward.) So, try your hardest to either hold onto your trash until you see a trash can, or store it in your running belt or vest for the time being, says Warshowsky.

“Without them, there is no race,” says Warshowsky. If a volunteer is giving you a directive—asking you not to step off the marathon race course to say hi to your friends, for example—don’t fight back. “It's not just about you, it's about the whole collective and everyone there,” she adds. They’re just doing their job and trying to keep everyone safe.

Remember: When you’re racing recreationally, these races are individual. “It's you versus you,” says Warshowsky. But it’s important to “be mindful of the people around you and how much time, preparation, energy, money, scheduling everyone around you had to go through as well as yourself.”

Run Your Next Race Even Faster With This 4-Week Plan

On a deeper level, remember that unless racing is your profession and there’s money on the line, “it's not always that serious,” Warshowsky adds. “The safety of yourself, your body, and the safety of everyone around you is more important” than a PR. If after a few miles—or workout stations—you know it’s not your day to beat your record, hang back, relax, and enjoy it. Remember why you race, and make it an enjoyable experience for yourself and everyone around you. There will always be another race where you can try your best.

#5037. It Just Got Easier to Get Peptides in the US. Here's What Could Come Next.

Spoiler: More access doesn’t necessarily mean more safety.

ON WEDNESDAY, THE U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced a new policy that makes six experimental peptides more readily available. According to a document released by the HHS, the government will not penalize specialized pharmacies for making and supplying these popular substances to patients with a prescription. The peptides: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500.

This does not mean these particular peptides have been approved for use by the FDA. In fact, none of them have gone through the rigorous human testing required for FDA drug approval. And the new policy is not intended to be permanent. Instead, it allows temporary access as the FDA decides on a longer-term plan for the six peptides. It also includes the caveat that compounders report “serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded,” according to the document.

This topic has been red-hot since July, when the FDA held an advisory committee meeting to consider whether to add these peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply. These substances are already widely used and obtained on the gray market. If people are going to use them, advocates have argued, it would be safest if those substances came from licensed pharmacies and are used with physician oversight.

Critics, on the other hand—including FDA scientists—are concerned that the government may be opening the floodgates to under-studied and potentially harmful drugs. These substances, they note, have not been fully vetted for safety and effectiveness. And some of these peptides are already being promoted and sold on the basis of scientific claims that experts say are unsupported or questionable.

Here's what could come next, if you're thinking about taking one of these six compounded peptides.

Some parts of the current conversation played out at last month’s PepMed conference in Washington, D.C. A sign pointing guests to the registration table featured a stylized gold peptide overlaid on the white dome of the U.S. Capitol. PepMed’s organizer, the American Academy of Peptide Medicine (AAPM), founded just last year, has already become a major voice in this debate.

In advance of the FDA’s July meeting, AAPM submitted hundreds of pages to a crowded public docket, including information about each of the seven peptides then under review. Several of its advisory board members spoke during the meeting’s public comment sessions. And the group appears to have the ear of the administration. PepMed speakers included the assistant secretary for health, Admiral Brian Christine, and a host of prominent MAHA figures.

The September event opened with an on-the-record media hour, featuring a dozen speakers, including physicians and owners and CEOs of compounding pharmacies and telehealth companies. A recurring theme was the danger of the gray market, where peptide quality can be difficult or impossible to verify and consumers often make treatment decisions without medical oversight—“this is not a victory for patient safety,” said Ricardo Rossello, PhD, a U.S. congressional delegate for Puerto Rico and AAPM advisory board member who co-founded Beijing Prosperous Biopharm, a medical research company.

Many of the speakers also lamented the failure of the U.S. health care system to fully meet the needs of patients, and some of the day’s speakers, including Alex Tatem, MD, an Indiana-based urologist and men’s health specialist with a large YouTube following, presented experimental peptides as part of the solution. “Our established medical system is very much a sick care model,” said Tatem, who serves on the AAPM’s medical advisory board. It’s important to help patients in a health crisis, he told me in an interview. But people want to be proactive about disease prevention. In his view, the peptides under FDA’s consideration can play a role by expanding “the toolkit that’s available to providers.”

At the FDA’s July advisory committee meeting, the agency’s scientists advised against allowing broad access to these peptides, in part because they have not been fully vetted for safety and effectiveness in the kind of long-term, rigorously designed human studies typically required for drug approval.Even at the conference, some doctors acknowledged the evidence gaps. Abud Bakri, MD, works in California as a physician who specializes in caring for hospitalized patients. He also runs a separate medical practice focused on preventive and longevity medicine, and he serves on the Enhanced Games Independent Medical Commission. His interest in peptides has been long-standing enough to predate his medical career.

Bakri, now 33, has been a powerlifter since he was 17. He explained that he has a genetic condition that may increase his risk for ligament injuries. He first used BPC-157 almost a decade ago, and believes the peptide helped him recover faster, though he acknowledges that this is hard to prove definitively, given the absence of well-designed human studies.

If just a fraction of the rat and Petri dish research holds up in humans, BPC-157 could be an incredibly helpful drug in the ICU, he told me at the conference, during an interview at an outdoor dining area. But ideally, he says, its effectiveness should be proven before it’s used in this setting and potential side effects should be better understood. “If I’m going to have an honest conversation with a patient,” he said, “I need to be able to fully elucidate the risk, which I can’t for some of these compounds.”

After the conference, I spoke by Zoom with Thomas Kremen, MD, a physician at UCLA Health who works for several athletic teams, including the Los Angeles Chargers and Lakers. Kremen and his colleagues recently reviewed the evidence behind six popular experimental peptides. He and his co-authors seemed unimpressed. “It’s probably not a strong stance to be recommending these things,” he told me.

Would it be accurate for physicians to tell their patients that a peptide like BPC-157 heals tissue?

“Maybe if they're talking about a rat in some study,” he said. “But I think if you're making a claim, you better be able to cite the literature that supports that.”

Right now, not only is there a dearth of high-quality clinical evidence that peptides work and are safe, unsupported claims are being made about these compounds.

For instance, among the documents that AAPM submitted to the FDA’s public docket was a white paper claiming that two experimental peptides—epitalon and BPC-157—are endogenous, indicating they are naturally produced by the body. Similar descriptions can be found on websites for telehealth companies and online peptide vendors suggesting their products are synthetic versions of naturally derived peptides.

Epitalon is a lab-made peptide based on an extract that researchers in the Soviet Union obtained from cattle brains. Terry Roberts, PhD, a researcher who studies epitalon at Brunel University of London, said it’s unclear whether humans produce this peptide. As far as he’s aware, no studies have explicitly described its presence in humans.

And BPC-157? The peptide was discovered in gastric juice, said Vince Luca, PhD, a researcher at the Moffitt Cancer Center in Florida. Yet 35 years after its discovery, nobody has found a gene that encodes for it—it could have come from a microbe or from food. It’s not impossible that the body produces BPC-157, said Luca, but he thinks it’s unlikely. He also says that health care professionals “should know enough not to tell [people] that it's an endogenous peptide” when it is very unlikely to be one. And regardless, he continued, “there are plenty of endogenous peptides that, injected at high concentrations, would have a really negative effect on the body.” In other words, being endogenous alone doesn’t mean it’s safe.

(The American Academy of Peptide Medicine’s press team did not respond to queries asking how the group determined that BPC-157 and epitalon are endogenous.)

“My prediction is that those who are already using the gray market will continue to do so,” said Ryan Beattie, director of business development at Adaptog Research & Life Sciences, a UK-based company that sells experimental peptides. “So I think in the initial term, people will use compounding pharmacies in the US. What I then predict will happen is people will then get used to it, get more aware of it—and then switch to the gray market because of the cost.”

He may be right. For this story, we spoke with two peptide users who had been living with chronic pain, and after trying physical therapy as well as other treatment approaches, turned to the Wolverine stack, a combination of BPC-157 and TB-500. Both said they felt the peptides helped them—and neither was sure they’d switch to compounded versions, which are more expensive than the gray market and aren’t covered by insurance. One of them, Charles A., asked, “What are the hoops and what are the costs going to be?”

A third person, who asked to be referred to as James—the name he uses in online communities—tried an oral version of BPC-157 four years ago and said he hasn’t been the same since then. Shortly after taking the experimental compound, he felt anxiety followed by sensory and emotional numbness that still hasn’t gone away. He also developed an autoimmune condition. Online, he found others with some similar experiences. When he looked carefully at the published research, he concluded that it didn’t match the online hype. “I felt very foolish afterwards.”

Some scientists are continuing to investigate these peptides. At Moffitt, Luca is currently studying BPC-157 and he’s keeping an open mind.

Over the next few months, he and his colleagues plan to run a variety of very basic experiments in which they add the peptide to human cells and see how those cells respond. The results could provide additional insight into what, precisely, this molecule is doing in the body—and they may help explain why users have reported everything from striking benefits to lasting harm.

Perhaps one day, BPC-157 will prove to be an effective drug, said Luca. But for now, his advice is to wait on using it and other experimental peptides: “I just worry that people are a little too cavalier in how these are handled.”

Sara Talpos is a Michigan-based journalist covering biomedical research and public health. She’s written for publications including STAT, Science, and Undark, where she’s a contributing editor.

#5036. Morning Minute: CFTC Clears Stock Perps, Gets Sued the Same Day

Morning Minute: CFTC Clears Stock Perps, Gets Sued the Same Day

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

⚖️ CFTC Clears Stock Perps, Gets Sued the Same Day

A perpetual future is a leveraged bet on a price that never expires. You hold it as long as you can meet margin and keep paying a funding rate. It’s analog product would be options in TradFi, with a few differences (primarily no expiration date). Crypto traders have used them for years, mostly on offshore venues like Binance and onchain platforms like Hyperliquid, because U.S. law had no clear home for the product.

On Tuesday the CFTC said Americans can now trade them on individual stocks.

Hours later, Wall Street sued to stop it.

The approval came as a statement from CFTC Chairman Michael Selig. Equity perpetual futures are now tradable on CFTC-registered exchanges, classified as security futures products under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000, which puts them under joint CFTC and SEC oversight.

The list of venues that can actually do this is short, and it was assembled quietly. A firm needs to be a CFTC-designated contract market and separately notice-registered with the SEC as a national securities exchange for security futures products. Seven entities hold both today: Cboe, CME, Coinbase, Kalshi, Bitnomial, Nadex, and ICE Futures U.S. Five of those seven filed inside a single 30-day window in September.

Kalshi is furthest along, with a filing covering 56 to 58 names and a launch expected within days. Coinbase has filed to list perps on Apple, Tesla and Nvidia. So those two are immediate winners. But Hyperliquid and Lighter, the top crypto perps protocols, are next in line for potential CFTC approvals and are likely future winners as well (LIT +10% on the day).

Then came the lawsuit. A new group called the Capital Markets Alliance filed in the Southern District of New York, naming Cboe, Citadel Securities and the Healthy Markets Association among its members. Its argument runs on two tracks.

The group wants the policy eliminated. The American Securities Association piled on separately, pointing out that Congress banned selling security-based swaps to retail investors at all.

A CFTC spokesman called the suit “troubling,” adding that “our markets should be governed by law, not litigation campaigns intended to block innovation.” The CME already tried this once, suing over the CFTC’s crypto perps approval on the theory that perpetuals are swaps rather than futures. That one went nowhere.

Well, remember that old phrase: “First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win."

We’re at the fight stage. Next stop, winning.

#5035. Binance hackers move 81% of stolen Solana, route funds via THORChain

The Binance attackers moved most of the stolen SOL and continued laundering funds through THORChain after the protocol resumed swaps.

The attackers behind the $6.3 billion Binance hack have moved about 81% of the stolen Solana (SOL) as they continue laundering assets through the cross-chain swap protocol THORChain.

Wallets grouped under the Binance hacker entity held 182,443 SOL (worth $16.9 million), or roughly 18.8% of the total 970,522 SOL stolen during the exploit, according to blockchain data platform Arkham.

Lookonchain reported on Wednesday that the attackers split SOL across multiple wallets, selling it for USDC, bridging to Ethereum to buy Ether, and ultimately swapping ETH for Bitcoin (BTC) via THORChain.

Binance suffered a record-setting hack on Thursday after attackers compromised employee devices through fake job interviews and malicious software downloads, the exchange said. Binance said Tuesday it replenished 98% of affected tokens and would absorb losses.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers on Saturday and urged crypto service providers, including THORNode operators, to block transactions linked to stolen assets.

Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, dismissed the accusations as “absurd rhetoric.”

North Korea-linked hacking groups are suspected of using THORChain to launder proceeds from some of the largest cryptocurrency hacks, including the $1.4 billion Bybit hack.

THORChain restored trading on Bitcoin, Ethereum and several other chains on Wednesday. Services had been halted on Saturday after an Ethereum block reorganization exposed a refund bug. The halt inadvertently delayed Binance hackers’ laundering activity, according to Chainalysis.

Blockchain investigator SomaXBT estimated that about 54% of the attackers’ more than 47,600 transactions on Tron and Solana were automated.

Binance hackers expanded their laundering activity to Solana on Sunday after emptying most of their temporary holding wallets on Tron. Chainalysis estimated that about $500 million in total value moved through Tron, including repeated transfers between wallets.

#5034. Democratic sweep of Congress forces crypto industry to rethink Washington strategy

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

As results rolled in, crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto said 19 pro-crypto lawmakers in the Senate had been elected and 226 in the House as Democrats took control of the House and Senate.

After two years of a pro-crypto, pro-innovation climate in Washington, the digital asset industry faces a sharp political jolt as Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress, forcing the sector to seek new allies within a party that has been more divided on crypto.

As results rolled in on Tuesday, crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto said 19 pro-crypto lawmakers in the Senate had been elected and 226 in the House as Democrats took control of the House and Senate. Eight anti-crypto Senators were also elected alongside 106 in the House.

Following the results, some in the crypto industry have taken the position that crypto is bipartisan and that lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are pro-digital assets. But a Democratic sweep means more oversight, and there is close to no chance of the crypto industry getting legislation it wants on the table.

"Nobody has their head in the sand," said Kara Calvert, vice president of U.S. policy at Coinbase, in a post on X. "There will be headwinds for any bipartisan legislation next year, but crypto is 100% bipartisan."

Many of the new members in Congress are pro-crypto, said Kevin Wysocki, head of policy at Anchorage Digital.

"The younger members are more used to this technology, are more open to new technology that maybe rivals some of the existing technology," he said in an interview with The Block on Wednesday. "It's very bullish, I think, for crypto overall, so I think that's one of the great things from what happened yesterday, and I think it's only going to get better over time, regardless of who's in power, Republicans or Democrats."

However, one of the biggest races the crypto industry had its eyes on, and money on, was the Ohio Senate race between former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown and SWC-endorsed Republican Sen. Jon Husted. The crypto political action committee spent tens of millions of dollars on that race against Brown, but ultimately lost when Brown defeated Husted later in the night.

Brown was previously Senate Banking Committee Chair, which has jurisdiction over digital assets and has been viewed as critical of crypto. He could have a leading role in oversight and regulation of the industry. And since he won in a special election to fill Vice President JD Vance's Senate term, that means Brown could return to the Senate as early as Dec. 15.

Brown's return is significant, Wysocki said. When he was chair of the Senate Banking Committee, Brown and his Senate staff were open to constructive conversations about crypto, he said.

Pro-crypto political action committees reportedly spent over $60 million alone in the Senate race in Ohio against Brown. On its own, crypto PAC Fairshake raised $106.2 million, according to Americans for Financial Reform. And crypto PACs overall spent $170 million on the midterms, according to Fortune, with millions going to Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska.

Fairshake spent $154.5 million in both primaries and the general election, with over $13.5 million going to Ricketts.

"Fairshake played a meaningful role in winning competitive races across the country in 2026 and we will do it again in 2028," said Geoff Vetter, spokesperson for Fairshake, in an emailed statement to The Block. "Newly elected and current members will have a choice: protect consumers and American jobs or fight progress. We will be watching and '28 is a new map."

One crypto industry source alluded that PACs and trade associations will have to "recalibrate" and need to "double down on being bipartisan."

Specifically on Fairshake, the person criticized funds being used on Brown's race.

"What did we ultimately get out of that?" they said. "Where could that money have been better spent? To be perfectly honest with you, I think it could have been better spent on shoe-leather lobbying."

That money could have been spent to lobby lawmakers on the Clarity Act, broad crypto legislation that passed the House, but got stuck in the Senate in September, they said.

"You spend a fraction of it, and you could have effectively hired all of DC to lobby on Clarity," they added.

Focus will turn to taxes and security and hacks, Anchorage's Wysocki said. The election, too, comes just days after the largest crypto hack on record of Binance for over $6 billion.

"Congress is going to be asking those questions, like how do we make security at our financial institutions stronger?" Wysocki said.

The Clarity Act that passed out of the House last year and stalled in the Senate a few months ago is unlikely to advance over the next two years given Brown's win, said investment bank TD Cowen.

Oversight will also come into view, including investigations into Trump-family-run World Liberty Financial, said TD Cowen’s Washington Research Group, led by managing director Jaret Seiberg.

"Democrats will investigate Trump's crypto entanglements, including World Liberty Financial," Seiberg wrote in a note on Wednesday. "We believe the resulting political environment may make it impossible to advance a version of Clarity that the crypto sector could back."

#5031. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Confirms Cyberattack After ZachXBT Ties It to $133M Crypto Theft

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Confirms Cyberattack After ZachXBT Ties It to $133M Crypto Theft

French banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed that it was hit by a cyberattack that allowed fraudulent operations, a day after onchain investigator ZachXBT named it as the alleged victim of a crypto theft of more than $133 million.

In a statement shared with Decrypt on Wednesday, the bank said the incident was "closed and now under control," and that operations were resuming gradually after it put stronger security measures in place. It said customers' assets were not affected, and that the attack had only delayed the execution of some transfers.

The bank did not mention crypto or say how much was taken. The amounts affected are still being assessed, but are "in any event not of a nature to call into question the solidity and financial health of the group," it said, according to Decrypt's translation.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said it informed the relevant supervisory authorities as soon as it detected the attack, and temporarily suspended some transactions as a precaution to prevent further fraudulent movements. It also warned customers to watch out for phishing attempts following the attack. Decrypt has reached out to Crédit Mutuel Arkéa for further comment, including on whether the losses involved crypto.

"Disclosing the EU financial institution exploited for $133M+ is allegedly Credit Mutuel Arkea, a French bank with $235B in assets," ZachXBT wrote on his Telegram channel on Tuesday. "The attack on the bank occurred for multiple days. I suspect the amount stolen is larger when accounting for OTC activity."

In an update on Tuesday, he said he had identified a further $27 million in exchange withdrawals by the attacker, bringing the total to more than $133 million, and that some of those withdrawals took place after his initial disclosure. He also published four Ethereum addresses he said were linked to the theft.

"My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it's currently being covered up," ZachXBT wrote at the time, accusing it of not having conducted "proper incident disclosure" and thereby preventing law enforcement from freezing some $30 million in stolen funds.

He did not say how he had identified the bank, or how the attacker gained access to its exchange accounts.

The mutual banking group has been preparing to move into crypto. In May, French financial newspaper L'Agefi reported that it had applied for a license under MiCA, the EU's crypto rulebook, to offer crypto services to its retail customers and to provide them as a white-label service through its Arkéa Banking Services division.

The allegation comes days after the $6.3 billion hack of Binance, the largest crypto theft on record, which the FBI has attributed to North Korean hackers. ZachXBT said the attacker in the suspected EU theft remains unidentified, but that he could say "with a high degree of confidence it is NOT Lazarus Group," the North Korean hacking collective, "based on multiple laundering indicators."

This story has been updated to add comment from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.

#5030. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa confirms cyberattack after ZachXBT flags $133M in suspected losses

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa did not confirm the exact amount of losses but validated the order of magnitude of the $133 million figure flagged by ZachXBT.

French bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed that a cyberattack enabled fraudulent transfers from its account, which were converted into crypto via specialized platforms.

In a statement released Wednesday, the bank said that client assets were unaffected and the incident has been contained.

"As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent movements against Crédit Mutuel Arkéa," the bank said.

"We wish to reassure all of our customers: this incident has had no impact on their assets," the bank added. "It only caused a delay in the execution of certain transfers."

Onchain sleuth ZachXBT, who first publicly flagged the exploit on Nov. 2, estimated the losses at more than $133 million. He noted that the figure could rise, as the attack unfolded over several days and may have involved additional over-the-counter transactions.

While Crédit Mutuel Arkéa did not confirm the exact amount of losses, it validated the order of magnitude. The bank said some of the stolen funds had been blocked.

"While it is therefore still too early to communicate a final amount, we can already state that the amounts involved are in no way of a nature to undermine the financial strength and soundness of Crédit Mutuel Arkéa," the bank said.

ZachXBT previously reported that the attacker had been moving stolen funds through a series of transactions, including swapping USDC for ETH, routing assets through instant exchanges such as WellWallet and Kyrrex, converting funds into XMR via Wagyu, and bridging assets across multiple chains.

He also said he has a "high degree of confidence" that the attacker was not associated with North Korea's Lazarus Group.

The bank has over 12,000 employees and more than 5.8 million members and customers. Its reported total assets are €211.5 billion ($238.1 billion), according to the statement.
